subtopic: REGISTERED TRAP LINES-RIGHTS OF CANADIAN ESKIMOS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Lesage (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: REGISTERED TRAP LINES-RIGHTS OF CANADIAN ESKIMOS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for Mackenzie River (Mr. Hardie) asked me the following question:
Is it true that Alaskan Eskimos living in the Mackenzie river delta hold registered trap lines, while there are a number of Canadian Eskimos who are without trap lines. If so, is the minister's department giving consideration to the prior right of Canadian Eskimos in this regard?
In answer I would say that the provisions with regard to the registration of trap lines are established by the council of the Northwest Territories and are set forth in the game ordinance, which became effective on June 30, 1949. They are not determined by the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources. The ordinance does not provide for any priority as between Alaskan Eskimos resident in Canada and Canadian Eskimos. However, under its provisions no Alaskan Eskimo who has entered Canada since June 30, 1949, or who may in future enter, can obtain a certificate of registration for a trapping area. No change in the position is contemplated at the present time.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a question of the Minister of Labour. Is he in a position to answer the question I asked a week ago?

speakeroldname: Hon. Milton F. Gregg (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO RE-EMPLOYMENT OP TEXTILE WORKERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was not hoping that my hon. friend would forget the question, but it was perhaps that I was not prepared to give an answer in exactly the way he might expect it.
However, in answer to the question he raised, I would say that the principal activity of the government in assisting workers in the areas referred to by the hon. member to secure alternative employment is the work of the national employment service, which comes under my jurisdiction.
When any worker applies to his nearest employment service office for employment, a full record is taken of his work experience, and this information is available in matching men with jobs not only in the immediate locality, but in Canada as a whole. This means that when employment opportunities develop in other industries and those applying for work have suitable qualifications, the applicants are referred to them. This applies to alternative employment opportunities which develop in their own immediate areas or to those which become available in other areas, if suitable workers are not available locally.
The hon. member will understand that there are many factors involved in the development of alternative employment opportunities in textile centres. I am sure the hon. member and I know some of those difficulties at quite close range. Aside from the work of the national employment service and other activities of the federal government, the government of Ontario has announced its intention to explore the possibilities of attracting new industries to centres in this part of the province. And I might tell my hon. friend that my department has expressed its desire to work in the closest possible co-operation with that project.

Mr. Speaker, while we are on the subject of microphones, perhaps I might deal with a question asked yesterday by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) and the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) having to do with the proposed purchase by two private companies of the government telephone and telegraph facilities in the province of British Columbia.


The target date for the transfer of the British Columbia Telephone Company to the Canadian National Telegraph Company is April 1, 1954. Unless there is some difficulty over which we have no control, I hope it will be possible to conclude the agreement by that date.
On the matter of transfer, there has been thus far satisfactory progress, and the maximum effort is being made by both these companies, the British Columbia Telephone Company and the Canadian National Telegraph Company, to work out means of absorbing the personnel employed at the present time. I am not in a position now to make a complete statement, but I shall make a full statement when the matter of the transfer is ready.
On the question of the survey that my hon. friend referred to, if he had in mind the appraisal which was made jointly by the British Columbia Telephone Company and the Canadian National Telegraph Company and the officers of the government, then I have no objection to his seeing it. I may say to him, however, that it is a voluminous and highly technical document. speechtext: Hon. members will find the item on page 51 and the details on page 430.

Just prior to the adjournment of the house last night I was commenting upon certain administrative and policy changes in the Department of Public Works which would at this stage seem to suggest that five public works projects for Alberta which were approved by parliament on May 9, 1953, have now been abandoned. These projects were at Claresholm, Coleman, Innis-fail, Lac la Biche and Vermilion. Being a confirmed optimist, and having complete faith in people, I had expressed the hope that under vote No. 401, which provides an appropriation of half a million dollars for advanced planning of projects including acquisition of sites, the aforementioned projects would be proceeded with. Either that, sir, or that provision has already been made to include those five projects in the supplementary estimates for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1955. Whether or not I am to continue to be a confirmed optimist will depend entirely upon the information which the minister is able to give to me.
Last night I indicated that one of those proposed projects was in my constituency, in fact in my home town of Innisfail. Last night I indicated the various steps and procedures which had been followed in an effort to secure an appropriation for that public building in the town of Innisfail. I indicated that first the town council and the board of trade took an active part. It was my privilege to accompany them to Calgary to confer with the post office officials in the district office at that point. I have reason to believe, as indicated yesterday, that Calgary must have reported favourably upon this project, because the next information which I received was that the Post Office Department had
Supply-Public Works
placed the project in "A" category and were extremely hopeful that it would be proceeded with.
The Post Office Department obviously convinced public works that this was a desirable and necessary project, and in convincing public works they must have been able to convince the then minister of public works because, as indicated before, these five projects, more specifically the one that I am primarily interested in, were included in the supplementary estimates for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1954.
May I just make brief reference to that appropriation because it may be misleading to some hon. members. On page 26 of the supplementary estimates which were tabled in this house one year ago, under "Alberta" reference is made to "Vegreville public building, additions and alterations, $50,000". Then it says:
Acquisition of sites and preparation of plans for public buildings at Claresholm, Coleman, Innisfail, Lac la Biche and Vermilion, $80,000.
Then the total of $130,000 is given. Then it says:
Less estimated amount by which actual expenditure on all projects listed in these supplementary estimates and the main estimates will fall short of the total of amounts that may be required for each, $129,999.
Then there is a line under that and then the figure "$1". Really what this house voted was $1. If we were to leave it at that point the answer to my problem would be completely obvious. However, 1 must take the committee back to last May 9, at page 5053 of Hansard. On that date the hon. member for Macleod was discussing this matter. He and I had previously discussed this appropriation because, as I indicated before, two of these projects were to be located in his constituency. The hon. member for Macleod is reported as having said:
When does the minister expect that the work of acquiring sites and the preparation of plans for these buildings will be started? In asking that question there is one other point I should like to raise. In reality this is a vote of $1, but the items in the details show an expenditure of $50,000 for the building at Vegreville and the acquisition of sites and preparation of plans for several other buildings to the amount of $80,000, making $130,000 in all. Then there is a footnote indicating that this amount is less the estimated amount by which actual expenditure on all projects listed falls short of the total of amounts that may be required for such.
Therefore my understanding is that all we are voting is $1 and that in voting the $1 we are also voting approval of the projects listed to the amount of $130,000. It is also my understanding that the projects will be proceeded with if there is money to spare from other projects or if other projects do not cost the amount of money we have voted for them. Is that correct?

Supply-Public Works
Then the hon. member tor Macleod went on to say that he hoped the inclusion of these items in the estimates was not merely dangling carrots before the people. Then the minister of public works went on to say this:
I can put the hon. member right. First of all, the explanation of the $1 item is that it is to authorize the department to draw on the main estimates for the province of Alberta in the construction of buildings or acquisition of sites. We expect that the main vote will be sufficient to cover some of these projects, if not all of them.
Then further down the hon. member for Macleod in referring to the minister had this to say:
He explained to me on one occasion that he has a whole list of projects and that they go from the top to the bottom. There is a certain formula that they follow and I take it that the time has now come when these projects will be carried out. I do triist that the work of at least acquiring sites and making plans and preparations will go forward this year. Does the minister think they will go forward this year?
The minister of public works replied as follows:
I just wanted to say to the hon. gentleman that it is not the minister who approves of these; it is parliament as a whole which is asked whether we shall go ahead with these projects. Now, parliament has great confidence in the Minister of Public Works and if they give him that authority I will see that my officials, although not perfect, will proceed as hastily as possible with the different projects.
I realize that that was a former minister of public works who was speaking but let me emphasize that what he said was that parliament had approved of these projects when it voted that particular vote in the estimates. Parliament did that, Mr. Chairman. When the minister of public works said that parliament had great confidence in the minister of public works, he was referring to himself maybe, or maybe he was referring to the office. I would say that we have great confidence in the present Minister of Public Works and we trust that he will adopt exactly the same attitude as his predecessor adopted with respect to this matter.
Let me remind the committee again that no matter what has transpired in the interval, parliament did approve of these five projects. I trust that the minister has not considered this whole matter so lightly that he.found it easy to relegate the decision of parliament to the garbage heap. I am not suggesting that that has been done; I certainly hope that it has not been done.
It could be argued that perhaps the board of trade of the town of Innisfail, that perhaps the town council, that perhaps the member of parliament who lives in that town could have erred in assuming that we required a new public building. Perhaps the district post office officials in Calgary erred; perhaps


the Post Office Department here in Ottawa erred; perhaps the minister of public works erred; perhaps parliament erred. But if that is true what a formidable array of errors there were.
I am going to suggest to you that none of them erred. If an error was committed I am afraid we would have to charge the present Minister of Public Works with having committed it, because we would have to conclude that if these projects have been deleted he looks upon the decisions of all those groups that have been mentioned as being wrong, as being unjustified, as being unwarranted, et cetera, et cetera.
Maybe the Minister of Public Works would be interested in something. I had occasion to go back to my home town just about a year ago today. When I arrived there I heard a song being chanted by some people. I never could make out the exact words, but it seemed to go like this:
Shaw, no public building;
No Shaw, a public building.
That little ditty was being chanted by some of my friends who have never wished me evil except that they would like to see me defeated as a candidate. Otherwise they would not want to harm me at all. Nevertheless that is the ditty that was being chanted. Let me tell the minister and the government that I found myself in one of the most peculiar positions that a member of parliament could find himself in just a year ago. Those people who were chanting that ditty-
Swan song.

were trying to convince certain people, in fact what they were saying was that as long as Shaw was their member of parliament they would never get a public building in Innisfail. Do you know what I told the people. I said that in the 13 years I had been a member of parliament I had never had cause to believe that the government at Ottawa had discriminated against me or against my constituency because I happened to be a member of the opposition. I said that because I thought it was true.
At that time we had Liberals, by inference at least, actually charging their own government with discrimination while I, facing a Liberal as my most formidable opponent, was defending the government and defying them to produce one iota of evidence to prove their charge. After all, Red Deer constituency has had an opposition member for 32 years. I am not unmindful of the fact that when they needed a public building at Red Deer, $500,000 was spent. I was then, as now, the member.

What is my position today after having defended the Liberals, after having asserted that I was convinced that the Liberals believed in democracy, in the democratic right of people to choose whomsoever they desired to represent them? What am I to say after having stated to these people that the charge of the local Liberals was absolutely false, that the preparations had been made, that the minister had given absolute assurance that the project would be proceeded with and that parliament had passed it. There was not a dissenting voice in this House of Commons. Now I will be going back for the Easter holidays and I trust that the minister will have this in the supplementary estimates before I go home, because then I will not have to say, "I thought I knew them, but I do not."
This is not a matter that I want to drag around in the political sense at all. The members of the board of trade, the members of the town council, do not look upon themselves as being Liberals, Conservatives, Social Crediters or anything else, when dealing with community problems. They are interested in their community, they built up a case for a building and that case was carried through to this parliament. It was approved by this parliament and I am asking the minister to honour what parliament committed itself to. Otherwise perhaps he can indicate to me an item hidden somewhere in the supplementary estimates covering an appropriation to carry out that commitment by parliament. It is not just a question of a post office, it is a question of adequate quarters sorely needed by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, and adequate quarters for the V.L.A. in that community.
I shall not take up any more time of the committee, Mr. Chairman. I shall wait for explanations before I come to any final decision so far as my next action is concerned, but I would urge the minister to give me some indication-
The same old song.

Let me say to the hon. member that no matter what the song might have to be it will not worry me personally. In fact it may enable me to go back later and say, "Well, I guess you were right. I could not properly assess Liberals even after 13 years."
Certainly this is more than a joking matter; it is a very serious matter of principle. I have great confidence in the Minister of Public Works. I feel we can rely on him to honour commitments made by his predecessor in this respect and carry out the unanimous decision of this parliament as far as that project is concerned.
Supply-Public Works

Mr. Chairman, this is the administration item of the Department of Public Works and as hon. members know it has been customary to deal with the broad problems of the department upon this administration item. That is what I propose to do on behalf of the official opposition. There are several points to which I wish to refer and I would like the minister to take each of them into consideration when he makes his general reply. I hope he will deal with all of these questions I am about to raise.
The first one has to do with the annual report of the department. I do not know whether it is a coincidence, Mr. Chairman, but you will have noticed that earlier in the proceedings today the minister's parliamentary assistant tabled a loose-leaf typed copy of the annual report of the Department of Public Works for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1953. For all practical purposes we are asked to consider the estimates of his department on the basis of a report for the year ended March 31, 1952, almost two years ago. That, of course, is a most inefficient way for the department to do business. It is contrary to the laws of the land and I can only express the hope that this will not happen again.
The statute which governs his department is known as the Public Works Act. Chapter 228 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1952, section 34, reads as follows under the heading, "Report":
The minister shall make and submit to the Governor General an annual report on all the works under his control, which shall be laid before both houses of parliament, within twenty-one days after the commencement of the session, showing the state of each work and the amounts received and expended in respect thereof, with such further information as is requisite.
All too frequently ministers of the present government have ignored provisions for the tabling of reports which, in effect, means belittling parliament and handicapping hon. members of the house in their work.

Might I just say that that provision, while it is worded as the hon. member has correctly quoted, was put on the statute book at a time when it was contemplated that sessions of parliament would start after the new year rather than in the fall as at the present time.

That may be so, but even if this session had started about the middle of January the report would have been due early in February. This practice of ignoring the provisions for tabling reports is unfair to parliament, unfair to hon. members and unfair to the Canadian people. I realize the minister is new in his department so it would

Supply-Public Works
not be right to place all the blame on his shoulders, but may I repeat in all kindness that I hope it will not happen again.
So do I.
That is a pious hope.

The second point to which I wish to refer is that there is no indication whatever in the estimates of the Department of Public Works that it is adopting recommendations which have been put forward for many years to the effect that this department should no longer be by-passed by other departments in the construction of public works. The practice has grown up under this government whereby practically every other department of government constructs public works of various kinds. As I understand it, the intention right down from confederation has been that construction work done by the government should remain under the supervision of the Department of Public Works except under extraordinary conditions. The official opposition, and I believe hon. members of other opposition parties, have pointed out time and time again that this new practice is wrong and have urged that something be done about it. I hope that under the new minister a stop will be put to this practice.
I would like to refer the minister to the report of the Senate committee on finance which sat in 1952 under the chairmanship of my very good friend Hon. Thomas A. Crerar, who served in the House of Commons with great distinction for so many years. With regard to this practice of by-passing the Department of Public Works by other departments, I quote from page 342 of the proceedings of this committee which sat in 1952, two years ago. The proceedings are reported as follows:
We draw attention to the items in the civilian estimates that have to do with the construction or acquisition of buildings and works, their repairs, and their upkeep, and rentals for buildings which different government departments require. The total amount under these three items found in the public works department estimates is slightly in excess of 80 million dollars.
I point out that that is for the fiscal year 1952-53. The report continues:
The total for all departments of government under these items is in excess of 163 millions. Under the Public Works Act, the public works department of Canada has the responsibility of providing and maintaining all the public buildings and works required by the other civilian departments. It is true part II of the Public Works Act makes an exception to the effect that the governor in council "may at any time transfer the management, charge and direction of any public work, or any power, duty or function with respect to any class of works, whether public or private, which is assigned to or vested by statute in any minister or department, to any other minister or department." But surely

this was only intended to meet special circumstances, and was never intended to be used in the broad sense in which it is used today.
Senator Crerar's report continues:
From the figures just quoted, it would appear that other departments of government combined are directly spending more for these purposes than the public works department which is primarily charged with this responsibility. For example, the Post Office Department, which requires public buildings all over Canada, either through building or rental for post office purposes, and requires to have them repaired and maintained, has all this work done by the public works department, as was intended under the act.
That is one good mark at least for the Post Office Department which has been under such heavy fire during the present session. The report continues:
The question naturally arises, why should this not be done for other civilian departments of government? When, for example, the Department of Agriculture, or national revenue, or national health and welfare-
Fortunately all three ministers are in the house at the moment.
*-directly provides for their own needs by building, or rental or both, they have to provide their own architects, their own engineers, and their own servicing establishment generally. It certainly appears that this can have no other effect than duplication and overlapping and the inevitable general increase in costs that is bound to result from this practice.
And the report concludes on this particular matter-

The minister may laugh it off but I think this report is fairly sensible. This report concludes as follows:
There are exceptions in the case of departments which have services abroad. The office space and maintenance which they require abroad will be secured more economically by such a department directly. But practically all of these expenditures, to which attention is drawn, are within Canada and, with very few exceptions, as for example the maintenance of buildings and roads in national parks, we do feel that this part of the administration of our public business should be under public works.

That was two years ago. Let us look and see what attention the government has paid to that report. I have here the figures for the fiscal year 1953-54, which was the first year after the report. We also have, of course, the figures for the current fiscal year 1954-55. Both those sets of figures will be found in the "summary of standard objects of expenditure and special categories" which is in the little pocket at the back of the book of estimates we are considering.
For the year 1953-54 the Department of Public Works was voted approximately $81,700,000 for the building of public works. By the way, this item is known as "Construction or acquisition of buildings and works, including land". For the other civilian departments-that is excluding the defence departments-the amount was practically as much for buildings and works, $79,300,000, and for the defence department, including defence production, $286,400,000.

I wonder if my hon. friend would allow an interruption. I shall deal with this matter at greater length later but I would say that in many of these instances in which other departments carry the moneys in their estimates, the Department of Public Works actually carries out the project.

I had that view too, Mr. Chairman, but in this latest departmental report which covered the period ending nearly two years ago, we find that the amount of money spent by the public works department for works and buildings but voted for other departments was only $10,500,000. It is a long way from that figure to the figure of $80 million.
Then in the current year, this present year, if hon. members will refer to their estimates they will find that the Department of Public Works is being voted for works and buildings $79,200,000, approximately, and that other civilian departments are being voted for the very same objects $78,500,000. Again practically as much is being voted to the other departments as to the Department of Public Works. The defence departments are getting less than in the preceding year, namely $214 million.
Let us take a look at the departments that are the worst culprits in this regard for this year, the year 1954-55. Here they are. First there is the transport department, $33,700,000; and mind you there is some excuse for much of the amount spent by the Department of Transport for public works. Then the Department of Agriculture, the second worst offender, $10,700,000; national research council, $6,100,000; the fourth culprit, Department of Citizenship and Immigration, $5,100,000;

Surely the minister would like to have a few suggestions for improving his department?

Then there is penitentiaries, $1 million. Those are only the worst offenders. Practically every department in this estimates book is spending a great deal of money on works and buildings. I suggest that the time has come to stop this sort of business and for the Department of Public Works to do the building for this country. The result would be a reduction in the number of architects and professional men; in fact I am sure there would be a great saving to the country.
Now I should like to say a word about the works and buildings for defence. The defence departments get away with quite a lot. They can always say, "We are defending the country; leave us alone". They get away with that in the House of Commons as well as outside of it, and I think the time has come to have a look at what they are doing with regard to expenditures for works and buildings.
I find that, according to the public accounts-I cannot get the figures from the report of the Department of Public Works because we have not yet received that report-for the year 1952-53, shown at page 43, the Department of Public Works spent $81 * 8 million on works and buildings. Then going to the report of Defence Construction (1951) Limited, or rather to the report of the Minister of Defence Production, who is the minister responsible for that crown company, I find at page 2 that during the fiscal year 1952-53 payments made by Defence Construction (1951) Limited amounted to $220,120,000 for public works. In other words, they spent about three times as much as the Department of Public Works.
Before the war most of the construction for the Department of National Defence was done by the Department of Public Works. I know it was the Department of Public Works that put up the forts around Vancouver. I suggest that the time has come when the Department of Public Works should

Supply-Public Works
at least do a lot of this construction that is now being done under the Department of Defence Production. In any event this crown company, Defence Construction (1951) Limited, should report to the Minister of Public Works rather than to the Minister of Defence Production so that we would get as much responsibility as possible for works and buildings in Canada where it belongs, that is under the direction of the Department of Public Works.
The third point I wish to place before the minister is this. There appears to be no longer any pretence that his department or any agency of government has a shelf of employment projects. We have been led to believe down through the years that the department had, in a pigeonhole somewhere, a lot of plans for public works that were to be used to give employment. I believe that idea started with the dominion's proposals in August, 1945, known as "Proposals of the Government of Canada", and contained in the green book. On page 26 I find this:
To follow the program proposed, the dominion is making provision that:
(i)	all basic survey and research work on which an expended resources program depends be gone ahead with as rapidly as possible:
I stress this second paragraph.
(ii)	advanced planning of projects be carried out on a sufficiently large scale to have an adequate reserve at all times for the timing purposes of the dominion public investment program.
That was a fairly clear-cut statement of policy, and I think members of the opposition and the Canadian people were entitled to take from it that the department actually had or would set up a shelf of employment projects. Now, with the new minister, we find that is a will-o'-the-wisp. He made a speech in Montreal three days ago, and I am reading from the report appearing in the Gazette on March 10. The heading is, "Public Works aim not to relieve unemployment".
Montreal; works minister Winters last night rejected the idea that public works be used specifically to relieve unemployment.
A public project, to be of real value, should carry with it the prospect of contributing to the long-term growth and development of an area, he said in a speech to the Montreal amateur athletic association.
This dispatch goes on:
Public works themselves did not necessarily provide many jobs. An example was the $23 million Canso causeway linking Cape Breton island and the mainland of Nova Scotia. Less than 200 men were required to keep the project up to schedule.
The minister may be right or wrong in taking that stand, but I believe the Canadian people are entitled to know whether or not it is still the policy of this government to organize a shelf of employment projects or whether that plan has been dropped.

The fourth point has to do with the expenditures for the Department of Public Works contained in these estimates. Hon. members will notice that there has been an increase of about $6 * 5 million over the last fiscal year. In effect, there will be a far greater increase because the department has adopted this new policy of trying to put in the estimates only those projects which are to be constructed, and as I understand, it is only asking for enough money to pay for the portion of the projects that will be done during the fiscal year. In effect, therefore, there is a very large increase in the amount of money being spent by the department during this fiscal year. There are some items which I believe require an explanation from the minister.
Hon. members will note, on looking at this summary of standard objects of expenditure and special categories, the main increases under these items. First of all civil salaries and wages show an increase. I do not believe anyone can quarrel with that, because I presume the increase is largely due to the increases in salary which have been given to civil servants generally. I go on to refer to eight other items, and I should like the minister to explain why the increases are necessary in each one of these items.
First of all is professional and special services, which item is going up this year by approximately $100,000. Secondly, freight, express and cartage is going up $70,000. Office stationery, supplies and equipment and furnishings is going up $125,000. Materials and supplies is going up $250,000; repairs and upkeep of buildings is going up by $1,100,000. Hentals of land is going up by $340,000. I am giving the round figures. Repairs and upkeep of equipment is going up $125,000. Municipal or public utilities services is going up $300,000.
Now, these are all substantial increases, and I would ask for an explanation as to why it is necessary to come to parliament and ask for these additional amounts for these particular services.
My fifth point has been well illustrated by the hon. member for Red Deer. It is this. The estimates for the last fiscal year appear to have been padded and, I can only think, were padded for election purposes.
I would refer hon. members, for example, to page 439 of the estimates book, where we find the estimates for the architectural branch of the Department of Public Works for Newfoundland. We find there that the estimate for 1953-54 for Newfoundland was $717,000. From that there was deducted the estimated

amount by which the actual expenditure on all listed projects would fall short of the total amount that might be required for each, $67,000. This left $650,000 which the government said was going to be spent in Newfoundland in 1953-54. We find that what was actually spent was $61,000. Mind you, a portion of that amount for the period, from the end of December 1953 to March 31, is an estimate but the figure there for the estimated total expenditure for Newfoundland is $61,000. This is less than one-tenth of the vote after there had been deducted from that vote an amount which it was calculated might not be spent.
Now, to say the least, that looks suspicious. I may be wrong, but it certainly looks as though that estimate was padded. I do not know why it should have been padded unless it was for election purposes so that government candidates could hold out to the voters in these different constituencies the prospect that public works were to be built. They could say, "There is a vote for a building for so much, and will you please vote for the Liberal candidate.". The Nova Scotia vote will be found on page 440. The figures there are not as bad, with about 50 per cent of the amount estimated being spent. The figures for New Brunswick are bad too, and they will be found on page 441. The figures for Ontario are found on page 445, and there again they are bad, the amount spent being about half of the amount voted.
Next to Newfoundland, Alberta was the worst. Perhaps the government had to promise more there than it did in other parts of the country. The figure for Alberta is found at page 447. The vote was $2,680,000 and the amount deducted that they would not be able to spend was $379,999, leaving a balance of $2,300,001. They spent $460,000, or in other words about a fifth of what they voted. The figures for British Columbia, my home province, are much the same. The vote there, after making allowance for what could not be spent, was $4,050,000, and the amount actually spent was $2,056,000.
Those are the figures only for the architectural branch of the Department of Public Works. The same picture, although perhaps not quite so bad, is found in the engineering branch.
Then the sixth point I shall place before the minister-and he will be glad to hear that I have only nine-has to do with what are known as government contract regulations. These are regulations which were passed under the provisions of the Financial Administration Act. I would ask the minister to explain some of these provisions.
Supply-Public Works
In the first place, when the full regulations were last passed-and this was on December 29, 1953-there was a provision with regard to construction contracts. The provision covered only works to which section 36 of the Public Works Act did not apply. Section 36 of the Public Works Act is the section which requires the calling of tenders. Apparently when these regulations were first drawn up they did not interfere with what was done under the Public Works Act. However, now we find that on February 25, 1954, an order in council was passed deleting from these regulations reference to the Public Works Act. This would appear to be a case of by-passing that act. So that now all construction contracts, including public works contracts, can be let under these government contract regulations instead of under the Public Works Act.
I may be wrong in this, but I suggest it calls for an explanation by the minister. In connection with these government contract regulations we find that "tender" is defined in a peculiar way. Section 1 (i) of the regulations is as follows:
"Tender" means (i) in respect of a construction contract, a tender invited by public advertisement and (ii) in respect of a purchase or service contract, a tender invited by public advertisement or from a representative list or lists of suppliers.
That would seem to be a pretty broad definition of a tender when it can mean purchase merely from a list of suppliers, without any tender being called. Yet it is considered a tender. When the minister explains this I would ask him to tell us how these lists are made up.
For example, in Ottawa how has it been the practice to make up the lists? We hear rumours of certain firms being able to get on the list and of other firms not being able to get on. I think probably that system has existed in a good many other parts of Canada. I would like to know from the minister whether a stop will be put to that sort of business.
Mr. Chairman-
Perhaps they do not do that sort of thing in Fort William or, if they do, the hon. member does not know about it.
I know Fort William.

The seventh point is much the same. Is there to be any change in the method of buying and renting property by the Department of Public Works? On some occasions there seems to be a kind of mental telepathy between the department and some of its good friends around the country, when it comes to buying or renting buildings. We had a case in Vancouver a few years ago of

Supply-Public Works a building called the Alvin building, which was built by friends of the government, under an agreement with the government, then rented by the government and bought by the government at a price far higher than should have been paid. But those friends were sitting there in a position to be able to put up that building. It is true that it was done through a company; but of course they were all members of the company.
Then we have postal stations and letter-carrier depots in Vancouver in respect of which a similar situation prevails. That is, people who are actively engaged in Liberal party work have at least been able to rent buildings to the government-perhaps not personally, but through companies they control. Is there to be any change in that sort of business? We have a new look, supposedly, in the Department of Public Works-a new minister and a new deputy minister. Is there to be any change made in the method by which property is bought or rented?
The eighth point is this. Will the minister explain complaints contained, concerning his department, in the public accounts. These are complaints made by the Auditor General in respect of the public accounts for the year ended March 31, 1953, and the particular part to which I refer is found at pages 12 and 13 at the back of the book. I shall not go into them in detail, but I would point out that the first complaint refers to the department's having cancelled an account receivable without obtaining what the Auditor General considered a proper authority. The second complaint has to do with the return of a deposit which had been put up by a contractor. This seems to be the more serious, and the Auditor General has this to say:
During the spring of 1951 a firm was awarded six contracts for the supply of post office lock boxes. Delivery dates were stipulated, but the contractor failed to deliver on time. As a result, two contracts, involving $24,125, were cancelled in May, 1952, and the work awarded to another contractor whose price was $3,796 higher. Nevertheless, the security deposits of $2,412 given for due performance of the two contracts were, with the approval of treasury board, returned to the contractor. Parliament having directed that "good and sufficient security" be given for "due performance of the work within the amount and time specified for its completion", it would appear to follow that, when a contractor defaults in performance, the deposit becomes revenue and any adjustment, as an act of grace, should be recorded as a charge to a vote.
That seems to be a very reasonable complaint by the Auditor General, and I hope the minister will be able to assure us that this sort of short-cut is not now being followed by his department.
Finally, I would ask the minister to explain what is going on in British Columbia about the power development on the big bend of


the Columbia river. I ask that because in the last few days statements have been made, both in the British Columbia press and in the Ottawa press, to the effect that General A. G. L. McNaughton, who is, as hon. members know, Canadian head of the international joint commission, had been in British Columbia interviewing the minister of lands and forests there, Mr. Sommers. As a result of those interviews the people of our province have been told that there is to be a $400 million 600-foot high dam constructed on Mica creek on the big bend of the mighty Columbia river. It is to start within eighteen months, and it is said that it will give British Columbia an estimated one million horsepower and will take seven years to complete and open up vast development possibilities in the interior. There is a similar dispatch in the Ottawa paper.
These dispatches read as though this plan is all set to go. I am not criticizing the plan; I think the development of the Columbia power is a very worth-while project; but what I should like to know from the minister is just what truth is in these reports and what plan is under consideration.
It is of vital importance to him, not only from the angle of construction of public works but because this plan will flood quite a few miles of the trans-Canada highway. When we asked the minister last year whether the route of the trans-Canada highway was going to be changed he said no, it was to be around the big bend of the Columbia river. If his department is involved in it for no other reason, it is because he has charge of the trans-Canada highway development in the dominion. Therefore, when he answers the various questions placed before him this afternoon I hope he will deal with this particular question.
Those are all the points I have to place before the minister. I hope that this new look which the papers have been trying to give to the minister and his department in the last few weeks will turn out to be substance, not just fiction.

Just a brief word; I was one of those who were greatly pleased when the Prime Minister thought it wise to appoint the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg as the Minister of Public Works. I knew he would be quite fit to take care of himself physically or mentally for anything that the opposition had to throw at him, and I have not been disappointed. I can see him kneeling behind the base and catching every baseball that came, and that is what he has been doing. He has been catching everything and delivering it in such a way that the team, which is the people of Canada, can appreciate his

deliveries. It is seen in the way that he handles the housing question. He answered all questions, and he delivered the goods in such a way that it will be a credit to Canada.
I must say that I was greatly pleased when I had a delegation from Fort William come down and interview the minister in connection with projects in Fort William that we think we need and have been trying to get for some time. He received that delegation from the city council and the chamber of commerce courteously, and he answered them intelligently. He sent them away feeling rather comfortable, believing that they would get what they asked for. I would remind him and his officials that those two projects are, first, the breakwater in front of Island No. 2 that we have been after for 16 years. I am going to tell the minister now that I hope that I shall be long enough in this house to see that project carried on, and I do not feel like quitting for a while yet. But the sooner it comes the better.
The other project has to do with a public building. We are paying out over $30,000 a year in rent for dominion offices. We think that we should have those offices in one building which up to now would be tax free. I am just reminding the minister of these things. We do not want to push unduly at Fort William, but when the place is growing and growing and showing rather a progressive spirit but still not very conservative, we think we should get a start on those things, and I am looking for them.
There is just one project that I should place before the minister. Since he is an outstanding athlete himself and knows how to keep his body in shape, he knows he cannot keep his body in shape unless he has the means to do so. Anybody will admit that surplus fat is a deadweight on any individual, and it does tend to mental obscurity and lack of clearness. There should be some place around this House of Commons where one could do physical exercises. I would prefer it to be underground. Since there is lots of rock around here, a place should be blasted out for a gymnasium and swimming pool. In time of war it could be turned into a shelter. I know the minister will consider this favourably. I have been after it for a while. I know that hon. members who have got something on their chests would like to get it off. If they could go and punch a bag for a while instead of punching the opposition or the government it would do them good and it would keep their minds clear.
I should like to congratulate the minister on the way he handled the housing question and the ticklish question of the film board.

I am sure that, before he is through, not only will hon. members from British Columbia, who were doubters, change their minds, but other hon. members will congratulate him.

Before I start my remarks in reply to several hon. members who spoke, I should like to thank the hon. member for Fort William for his very kind references and to express the hope that I shall be able to measure up in some small respect to the high aims he has set for me.
In reply to the hon. member for Red Deer, who apparently has left the chamber, I would do no more therefore at this stage than remind hon. members that the vote for the architectural branch, which was the branch in question, in the estimates for the coming year, 1954-55, is an amount of $3,600,000; whereas the corresponding vote last year was $2,300,000. There is an increase of $1,299,999 for the province of Alberta alone, thereby indicating that there is no attempt whatever to discriminate on any grounds that might possibly have been in the mind of the hon. member. What we are trying to do is to apportion the money we have in such a way that we shall get projects in a place rather than simply notations in the estimates book that hon. members are dealing with now.

Would the minister at this time put on record the reason the change was made in these particular votes to which the hon. member for Red Deer made reference? Why was the change made after the house had voted them? It would be a good thing if that were on the record.

I dealt with that generally last night. The whole reason is that we are trying to evolve a system of including in the estimates just those projects that we are in a position to go forward with in the fiscal year in question. Some projects were not planned to the stage where we could go forward with them. Rather than put an amount in the estimates that did not mean anything and would just prevent us voting money for some other project that was ready to go forward, we had to consider the whole over-all program and just include this year those projects which we thought there was a good likelihood of doing something about. That does not mean that any project has been abandoned, but it does mean that each one must be considered on its merits and in relation to the relative urgency for having something done about the various projects in particular areas.

Supply-Public Works
Is the breakwater at Fort William all right?

That is another matter that will have to be dealt with on its merits, just as all other projects that are so dear to the hearts of hon. members.
I should like to deal now with the very good speech made by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra and compliment him upon the very thorough way in which he has studied the Department of Public Works, its estimates and also the role which he has in mind for this department. I am not in position to disagree with him in his remarks about the annual report except to make the qualification that when the statute placed a limitation as to the date parliament then had in mind that for the most part the sessions would be commencing after the new year rather than in the fall, as we have been doing recently. Therefore, the date pushes everybody pretty hard, but most of all the queen's printer. There has been a bottleneck there. Because of the statistical nature of the department's report it is difficult to assemble all the information. We did think that it might be helpful if we could put the report before hon. members today, even though it was in unbound form and even though it was not available to everybody. I thought it was better to do that than not to have it available at all. The printed bound copies I hope will be available to all in another two weeks. I hope in this respect we will be able to do better next year and we certainly intend to try to meet the requirements imposed on us by parliament.
For some years the hon. member has dealt with what he believes to be the proper role of the Department of Public Works in the general program of government construction. Here again let me hasten to say that I am not one to disagree with him. I think the general attitude of the government is that the time has come for the Department of Public Works to be re-established as the government's agency in the field of public works. The hon. member probably will recall that at the time the Prime Minister made the rearrangement of portfolios recently he transferred to the Minister of Public Works federal responsibility for the trans-Canada highway and Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, both of which enter largely into the field of construction, as well as certain other responsibilities formerly carried out by the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources.
We have been discussing with the Department of National Revenue, the Department

of National Health and Welfare, the Department of Transport and other departments the extent to which we can get the Department of Public Works in shape organizationally and administratively to take on a larger volume of public works. As an example, recently the Post Office Department applied for an additional architect and we told them that we thought we could provide the architectural services they required. They agreed not to take on the architect but to leave that work with the Department of Public Works. The Department of Transport is another department that is considering transferring some of its construction operations to the Department of Public Works.
Speaking on behalf of the Department of Public Works, I know hon. members would expect me to say that I would not want to take on a volume of work that the department was not capable of coping with. We have had the organization of this department under close scrutiny for the past five months. Hon. members are probably familiar with some of the changes that have been made. In the first place, the former deputy minister, Mr. Emmett Murphy, a very competent engineer, reached retirement age and subsequently took his retirement. He has been replaced by the former deputy minister of the Department of Resources and Development, and previously the vice-president of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. I have worked closely with this gentleman when he was in those two capacities. He was asked to accept the position of deputy minister of public works, which he did. Hon. members know the fine record of accomplishment of Major General H. A. Young in the service of his country, in war and in peace. I am very happy that he has seen fit to come to this department.
Just prior to the rearrangement of portfolios the chief architect, Mr. Gustave Brault, took his retirement and was replaced by Mr. E. A. Gardner, who is the present chief of the architect's branch. Shortly after I came to the department the then chief engineer, Mr. Robert Blais, reached retirement age and retired. We promoted to that position the assistant chief engineer, Mr. A. A. Anderson, who is now doing a very fine job of work. But he also is reaching that inevitable period of life when retirement seems to loom just over the horizon.
We are endeavouring to rearrange both the architect's and engineering branches of the department. We have applied to the civil service commission for and they have approved the establishment of a new position in the architect's branch to be termed director

of property management and maintenance. That position has been established, a competition has been held, and we hope shortly that the successful candidate will be designated. We are endeavouring to set up in the Department of Public Works another position of chief engineer. Having regard to the fact that we have undertaken the trans-Canada highway and additional construction operations we need this new position. We hope in due course to have the organization in shape where we can expand and take on additional public works which we believe are the proper function of the federal government.
When the department is able to assume these additional works, then I have no doubt that other departments of government will be quite prepared to have the Department of Public Works do them. No department wishes to undertake work of a nature, particularly if it duplicates functions being performed by some other department which on the face of it is more appropriately designed to carry out the functions. The hon. member spoke of a shelf of public works.

Before the minister goes on, may I point out also that I referred to Defence Construction (1951) Limited and suggested that that corporation should also come under the Department of Public Works and that the department should do some of the work now done by that corporation.

I think that is a suggestion that must be considered. I am sure that the hon. member knows that Defence Construction Limited has been having its construction contracts handled by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. While that corporation is not part of the Department of Public Works, it does report to the same minister. There is a close-knit arrangement of construction activities under the Department of Public Works and Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. However, the suggestion made by the hon. member is well worth thinking about.
I recall discussing a shelf of public works with the hon. member on previous occasions. There are great difficulties in endeavouring to build up a shelf of public works. I do not think a shelf was too good a concept right from the start. Planning for public works is not something that is static in a country which has been growing and expanding the way this one has. We have been very hard pressed to keep up with current planning, let alone get ahead far enough to put anything in such a dormant state as to have it rest on a shelf.
It does not seem a concept with which one can comply in an expanding economy under
Supply-Public Works
such buoyant conditions as we have been experiencing when considering at the same time the shortage of engineers, architects, and other technical assistants. We believe in the principle of planning ahead, and my hon. friend will see in the estimates that vote 401, to which I referred last night, asks parliament to make available to the Department of Public Works the relatively small sum of $500,000 this year to enable the department to acquire sites in the many small communities where we are obliged to operate from time to time, and to do some planning with respect to these sites without actually committing ourselves at that stage to carrying forward a public work. That is something I hope we can develop as time goes on because I believe it will make for more orderly planning, more orderly budgeting, and more orderly scheduling of work.
My hon. friend asks why expenditure had increased in a number of categories as set forth in this summary of standard objectives and expenditures and special categories of service charges, and more especially with regard to maintenance charges. I am sure if my hon. friend were in the position in which I am he would be struck by the increased costs which follow the construction of every new building. There are increases in maintenance, service charges, cleaning supplies, janitor services, window cleaning, general run of the mill maintenance and in all those other requirements which are a necessary part of our expanding program of public works. To the extent that we are going to be asked by parliament to build new buildings, then we must be prepared to meet increased costs annually for servicing these new buildings. It is true that we save on rentals. But when we acquire a property to be owned by the crown, then the crown must be prepared to pay the charges necessary for servicing it.
My hon. friend dealt with government contract regulations and stated that there were some changes in them with which I must confess I am not entirely familiar because I did not quite get the point he was making. I believe it had to do with the calling of public tenders and I would like to tell him that it is the policy of the department to call for public tenders wherever that is feasible. I am a very strong believer in that myself. I believe it is a fair way in which to do business in almost every instance and it is the best way to do business wherever it is practicable. My hon. friend will find that we do as a general practice call for public tenders for public projects.
2942

Supply-Public Works
He referred to purchases from a representative list of suppliers. There are instances where it is not feasible to call for public tenders for relatively small amounts of supplies, and it has been the practice in the past, and I presume it will continue to be the the practice regardless of what government might happen to be in office, to establish lists of reliable and competent suppliers and to invite tenders from them when it is not feasible to call for public tenders. In my experience that policy has been administered fairly and, I believe, in such a way as to protect the public interest.
My hon. friend asked if there was to be any change in the method of buying and renting property. At the same time he said he knew of many occasions on which properties owned by friends of the government were ultimately bought by the government. I would like to think that all citizens of Canada are friends of the government. If my hon. friend were to occupy the position in which I am, and he heard the comments of his own supporters in the house, I think perhaps he would not attach too much importance to the rumours he hears to the effect that it is only supporters of the government who can sell property to the crown. Hon. members on this side of the house have on many occasions held exactly contrary views, but it is the policy of the department to buy on merit, and my hon. friend well knows that people these days do not get rich by selling property to the crown.

There is to be no change,
then?

I do not know of anything
which would warrant a change in government policy and I am therefore not in a position to tell my hon. friend there will be a change. The policies which have been adopted and implemented by the government have been framed with the public interest in mind. But if my hon. friend knows of any instance where that is not true I would be glad if he would bring it to my attention.
My hon. friend's next point had to do with the Auditor General's report, and the hon. member mentioned two items in particular which evoked comment from the Auditor General. One had to do with the cancellation of a debt as an act of grace. I have quite a long answer in justification of that, but perhaps if I read the last paragraph it might satisfy my hon. friend.
The department took the stand (a) that it had not carried out its agreement; (b) that no service was performed and no value

received by the contractor and that no debt to the crown was incurred by the contractor. For that reason the crown took the action it did.
The other point in the Auditor General's report dealt with by my hon. friend had to do with the return of a security deposit to a contractor in default. In reply to that I would say the officials of the department did not feel that security deposits could be considered as revenue unless and until they had been forfeited. Forfeiture was considered too drastic in this case and the treasury board approved the charges made by the contractor in view of the fact that the practice followed was approved by the treasury board under section 36 (a) of the Public Works Act, as the cost was in respect of calling for tenders. That was an act approved by the treasury board.
The last point dealt with by my hon. friend was the proposed development of a large hydroelectric dam at Mica creek on the northwest corner of the Big Bend highway. That whole project is still under investigation by my colleague the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, who is responsible for the water resources division. My present concern is with the trans-Canada highway; and my hon. friend from Van-couver-Quadra quite rightly stated that if this dam, which I understand will be some 600 feet high, is built, then a substantial portion of the existing Big Bend highway will be flooded. The appropriate minister of the government of British Columbia, for some years before the present government took office and since, has been in communication with me in respect to this possibility. I told him that if he cares to go ahead with the construction of the Big Bend highway, and should it then be flooded out in whole or in part in that section, then his government would be completely indemnified for damages resulting from the flood.
I read with interest the report to which my hon. friend referred to the effect that the construction of this dam is more imminent than we imagined. I was somewhat surprised at the 18-month period mentioned. I would be inclined to think that it would be a little longer. However, studies are still continuing and there is a distinct possibility that a dam will some day be built there.

At the outset, Mr. Chairman, as a native son of the Red Deer district and a nephew of the man who put Red Deer constituency in the opposition camp some 32 years ago, I should like to say that my soul was somewhat stirred by the plea made

by the hon. member for Red Deer a short time ago and I wish him well in it.
I am glad that we have heard the Minister of Public Works make his statement. From various sources since the appointment of the present minister to the position he now holds we have been hearing that changes were afoot in respect of the Department of Public Works. I was rather disappointed when, at the outset of the debate, he apparently did not see fit to make a statement as to what his thinking was about the future of his department. I am extremely glad to note that he was able to overcome his natural modesty and to give us some outline of what he has in mind. I think I can speak for other members in this group as well as myself and say that, in the organization and the planning of that department, we will welcome any change which makes it a more effective instrument of national development rather than, as at times in the past it appeared to be, something of a chore boy for other departments of government.
In this connection, may I say I was interested to note that in this year's estimates the amount allocated for the trans-Canada highway had been increased from $15 million, as it was in last year's estimates, to $20 million and that the amount to be spent in the national parks had been doubled. To me that was an indication that the kind of development that I should like to see taking place within the public works department has some reality to it. I feel that in many ways that is one of the most important aspects of our national development which now come within the jurisdiction of the Minister of Public Works. In that connection I came across one or two statements which I found represented very closely my own thinking on the matter. These statements were contained in an address by Mr. William A. Wecker, president of General Motors of Canada, Limited. I should like to quote briefly one or two of his remarks in this connection, partly because I imagine that no hon. member would consider that he is simply a wild-eyed socialist visionary as some people might be inclined to consider me to be. In connection with the project of highway development his remarks in part were as follows:
. . . when confederation came into being ... it was quite properly believed that the railway would be the prime instrument of the country's development. that roads would be of limited local concern and should, therefore, be left entirely to the provinces to build and maintain. The fathers of confederation acted quite properly for their day and age. They were deliberating Just about 35 years prior to the appearance of the first motor car in
Supply-Public Works
Canada. And so roads have been principally the responsibility of small local governments and the provinces.
Then he goes on to say this, and I certainly agree with his sentiments in this regard:
. . . Roads have become a matter of national importance. Most major traffic routes connect cities in different provinces and carry traffic of two or more provinces. Eventually they will be largely interrelated and interconnected in a national pattern of highways.
. . . Roads are more than a provincial or municipal matter. They have become a national problem and must be treated nationally.
. . . We must have a broader area of co-operation and understanding among road building authorities.
He then mentioned what to me was an extremely interesting fact, namely that the tonnage of freight carried annually by motor transport in Canada exceeds the combined total of that carried by rail, water and air. He also mentioned that there are 14,000 communities in this nation which are chiefly dependent upon highway transportation for their very existence. He also pointed out that between 1915 and 1933 the number of motor vehicles in Canada rose from 60,000 to one million, that it took another 15 years for the second million vehicles to be added to the roads, but that in only 4 years prior to the time at which he gave this address-and that was on October 20, 1952-another million motor vehicles had been added. The point of that statement, I believe, is that it indicates the accelerating rate of increase in the number of vehicles, as a result of which highways are becoming of ever greater importance from the national point of view. Then he goes on to say this:
The Hon. Robert H. Winters, Minister of Resources, in a speech not so many weeks ago, probably touched the reason why the road builders are losing ground when he said that the volume of traffic on new highways is always greater than had been estimated.
So rapid has been the increase in Canada's motor vehicle fleet-we have added 50 per cent to it in the last four years, as I explained earlier-that neither Mr. Winters nor any other highway planner could be expected to forecast exactly the physical expansion required.
That may be perfectly true. In addition to that, I was much interested in the remark made by the minister to the effect that they are making provision for a certain amount of advance planning. As a result of their initial venture into this field, I hope they may be able to pursue that particular idea on a larger scale as time goes on. In relation to highway development, particularly in connection with the matter of planning, an example that occurred to me as an indication of how planning, if it was carried on in advance, could be of benefit, exists in my own riding where at the present time we have a great many excellent highways being

built by some of the larger logging corporations. As their understanding and knowledge of forest management has increased, they have more and more planned their highway building in advance of their current needs so that they are able to conduct a much more flexible and economic operation, viewed in larger terms. I feel that is one of the major problems facing us today. One of the ways in which a revitalized public works department can be of real national service is if the minister and also parliament can translate into a national concept some of the energy, initiative and imagination that a great many able executives today are able to put into their planning in connection with private corporations. I have long felt that this is going to be the secret of the future growth of Canada, that it is going to be the way we are going to avoid some of the problems we were discussing not long ago in connection with unemployment. If, somehow, the members of this parliament and the citizens of this country can achieve a method of making use of the type of initiative which you find in many great organizations today on a national scale, then we shall be successful. In my opinion that is the crux of the problem with which we are faced. Actually that is why I find myself sitting politically where I do in this parliament.
Perhaps I might have pursued this subject at greater length if the minister had not made the statement he did, which has given us some of his thinking and some indication that he does intend to pursue a policy of expanding and developing the department. Perhaps this will be not altogether along the lines I have suggested but at least some steps in that direction are going to be taken. I shall conclude this part of my remarks simply by saying I wish him well in that aspect of his work.
I believe there is a rather formidable roadblock in the way of developing his department along the lines he has suggested, and along the lines for which we are hoping.
I would illustrate that by saying that in the minds of the citizens of Canada, and I might go so far as to say in the minds of some of the members of this house, there is an unhealthy atmosphere surrounding the Department of Public Works. In my opinion that is one of the biggest problems facing the minister if he is going to carry out the kind of development he envisages for this department.
May I give an illustration of what I mean.
I am going to read from a column which appeared in the Campbell River Courier on Wednesday, August 12, 1953. This column


is written from week to week by the editor of that publication, and on that date he had this to say:
Election of C.C.F.'er Tom Barnett as member of parliament for Comox-Alberni came as no surprise to those who saw the anti-socialist vote split umpteen different ways . . .
I might just point out in passing that even the editors of newspapers in British Columbia who are not of my political persuasion recognize the essential unity between the various non-socialist groups. It is not quite as apparent in other parts of the country as yet.
And between the two socialist groups, too.

speechtext: The minister is fishing.
I am sorry, but I could not quite catch the interjection the minister made.
They recognize the same essential unity between the two socialist groups, the socialists and the communist party, as demonstrated by the recent speech of Mr. Rod Young.

I did not hear the recent speech by Mr. Rod Young to which the minister refers. I might point out to him from my own experience that I have not found any great love was bestowed upon me so far as a certain communist group he mentioned was concerned. Any question of unity, as he well knows, has never been a very prominent aspect of the relationship between those two political organizations in British Columbia.
Mr. Young told the students of the C.C.F. club at the University of British Columbia that there was no difference between socialism and communism.

I am sure the minister is acquainted with the gentleman to whom he refers, and I suggest he might discuss the matter with him the next time he is in British Columbia and find out what the gentleman really did say or what his views are on that subject.
He was a former C.C.F. M.P., and should know what he was talking about.

Getting back to editor

Thus, In a predominantly Liberal House of Commons, vve of this riding will be represented by a member of an opposition party and, things being the way they are in politics, we can look forward to a four-year drought in the matter of public works expenditures in tills constituency.

Mr. Barnett, we have no doubt, will do a good job of representing us. He will doubtless present our cases (as they come up) with earnestness and eloquence . . . but not persuasion. For he is not on the government side.
