I have taken the liberty of using that quotation to demonstrate that in the minds of many people there is what I have already termed an unhealthy attitude in respect of the Department of Public Works. As long as that attitude persists, as long as a lot of people consider that the public works department is supposed to be the Santa Claus of government, then I would suggest the hopes the minister has expressed for the development of his department are not going to come to fruition.
I recognize that he has a big job, and I recognize also it is not a job he can do alone. In fact I would say that the success of the job he might be able to do depends as much on the members of this house as it does upon the minister himself. I believe it will be necessary for members who are sitting on the same side of the house as the minister to exercise a great deal of restraint in making requests of the minister for special consideration for their particular constituencies. On the other hand, I would say that to succeed in changing the public attitude in regard to this department may mean that members on the opposition side will perhaps have to exercise some patience at times when they might be disposed to consider that there was discrimination against their constituencies.
I suppose my remarks expressing the hope that the minister will bring about a change in the atmosphere surrounding the Department of Public Works will be considered by some people as an example of political naivete. All I can say is that I hope I shall be able to retain a certain amount of naivete, and I would be quite happy to discover that the minister also has been able to retain a certain amount.
I do not intend to go into a long discussion of the details of the public works estimates at this time, particularly as they relate to the constituency of Comox-Alberni. I know there are occasions when such matters will be discussed between the minister and myself. However, I have attempted at, I hope, not too great length to set out the attitude and the viewpoints the minister can expect from this corner of the house in relation to the plans he has for his department.

Mr. Chairman, I listened with great interest to the statement by the minister, and felt he did everything he
Supply-Public Works
could to answer the questions raised. I have a question to raise; it was brought up last year and still remains in the category of uncompleted business. My question has to do with the construction work done by the Lunam Construction Company, operating for the Department of Public Works and other departments of government.
It will be recalled that when this matter was brought up last year there was a very lengthy discussion on the subject and, in particular, as to what could or should be done in order to protect subcontractors and suppliers of materials and commodities to contractors with government contracts. That problem still remains.
I want to ascertain from the minister what changes have taken place in that policy., for I find subcontractors in all parts of Canada who are very much concerned over the fact that, in accepting subcontracts from contractors with government contracts, in reality they assume a risk that is not assumed when they deal with private contractors. When they deal with private contractors they have the right to file mechanics' liens against properties within the limitations of the mechanics' liens acts of the several provinces. In this way they are able to protect themselves to the extent provided by those acts.
It is otherwise, however-and it has been so held on a number of occasions-with subcontractors who supply commodities or supplies of any kind to contractors having government contracts. In connection with the Lunam Construction Company of Regina the total of accounts of creditors of that company, which held a number of contracts with the Department of Public Works as well as with other departments of government, when it ceased operations amounted to $256,652. Comparatively small companies were involved to the extent of amounts such as $12,500, $10,000, $17,000, $6,000 and $14,700. Then there is one for $27,800 for heating supplies, and another of $37,500 for an electrical company.
I am not going over the story of the Lunam Construction Company. We all know what happened in consequence of certain revelations that were made. But I do think the problem still remains, and it is this. How can subcontractors in this country undertake, with a reasonable degree of safety, to make the necessary supplies available to contractors when those contractors have government contracts? In the case of the Lunam Construction Company I think anyone who is frank will admit that that company was allowed by the department to place itself in a position detrimental to the interests of
2946	HOUSE OF
Supply-Public Works
subcontractors who supplied the materials that went into the completion of that contract.
Under the regulations set out by the Department of Public Works this provision is made:
During the prosecution of any contract, as a progress estimate then being rendered shall show a gross total accomplished equal to or in excess of 30 per cent of the whole amount of the work contracted for, the contractor shall be required to furnish to the department a statutory declaration signed by himself, or some one of his employees who has personal knowledge of his business arrangements and accounts by which the department shall be assured that all his liabilities in connection with work under the contract up to and including the last previous progress estimate have been paid by him.
And this further provision:
As soon as the work under the contract shall be shown to have reached the point indicated in section 2-
That is the one I have just referred to.
-the contractor shall obtain from each ot his subcontractors a receipt tor payment of amount due under the terms of the said contract up to a date not more than one month earlier than the date of the then present progress estimate.
A form is provided for this purpose. I find upon examination of the records that this latter precautionary measure was not observed, with the result that subcontractors lost a tremendous amount of money because they dared trust that the government of Canada, in its contractual relationships with subcontractors, would live up to the provisions of its own regulations.
The minister says that changes in personnel have been made in the last year. I hope and trust that changes will be made that will not permit a similar state of affairs to exist again. And this is not a solitary incident; it is happening in other departments of government. It is happening in connection with Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. In one case in Vancouver creditors find themselves out of pocket to the extent of $225,000, with the hope of recovering only 20 per cent of that amount. And there are cases in other parts of Canada involving lesser amounts where subcontractors-local dealers, merchants, hardware men, lumber dealers, suppliers of pipe, brick, and the like-having trusted that the federal government would carry out its own provisions, have found themselves suffering tremendous losses.
Last year suggestions were made as to some things that might be done in order to remove this danger. It is unfair that the government of Canada should be able to take advantage of the small businessmen of this country by having their supplies used in the buildings that are being erected by contractors for the government, and at the same time failing to protect the suppliers


even within the limitations provided by the present regulations. After the discussion in the house last year in regard to the Lunam Construction Company I had correspondence from subcontractors in every part of the country, asking whether or not something could be done.
One of the suggestions is that a performance bond should be required on federal work in the same way it is required in connection with private industry. What changes have been made to provide protection to the subcontractors for payment of materials supplied on federal jobs, protection in lieu of the mechanics' liens that are available to contractors on other than government contracts? This is a matter that deserves serious attention, as the minister has pointed out, because of the expansion that is taking place in his department and the works that are to be carried out during the coming year. I feel that the subcontractors of our country have a right to know what is going to be done to protect them at least to the extent that protection would be available if they were dealing with private contractors on private business.
In connection with the Lunam Construction Company, was any arrangement entered into with any of those subcontractors whereby they have been given to understand that on any future tenders that they may make on other contracts, consideration will be given to them for part of the losses they suffered?
Is my hon. friend stating that as a fact?
I am asking whether it is so, because that is the rumour.
Can my hon. friend give me any basis for those rumours?
I say the rumour is quite widespread that something similar to what took place in connection with the Milk river project in Alberta is going to be done.
I was wondering whether my hon. friend has any substantiation for that.
The minister can say whether there is any foundation for it, whether it is a fact. He is the one with the information.
I say it is not a fact. I was asking if the hon. member had any substantiation for it.

That is the question I am asking. What is the position of those subcontractors? Are they to be taken for

a ride to the extent of almost $200,000 because they dared trust that the government of Canada would give them the same consideration they would be entitled to were they dealing with a private principal? After what took place last year, and the revelations in connection with the Lunam Construction Company, I ask the minister what changes have been made in his department and what alterations have been made in the regulations? In connection with the Lunam Construction Company, I should like to know why no prosecution of Mr. Lunam was ever instituted for the false declaration in which he swore that the various suppliers had in fact been paid by him? What has taken place during the last year in that regard?
The minister will recall that his predecessor found a great deal of difficulty in finding Lunam. The search went on for two or three months; then a reporter, Miss Judith Robinson, went to Regina and was able to find him on her arrival. What is the present position in that regard? Have any proceedings been taken on the declarations which the minister's predecessor said were false? If not, is any action contemplated at the present time? I ask those questions because in this case, as in the case of the Vancouver Associated Contractors Limited, good citizens, local merchants, suppliers of all kinds, are being placed in a position where they have a perilous future if they dare to trust any contractor who has a contract with the Department of Public Works or with any other department of government, for the supplying of goods, wares and merchandise. This is a matter which I believe requires the utmost consideration by the officials of the department.
The minister has taken over this department. He has brought with him a deputy minister who enjoys the respect of all who know of the work he has done in the past. I feel that this is a most important matter and requires action, because a repetition of the Lunam Construction Company case, though on a smaller scale, has taken place in two or three instances in connection with government contracts.
I ask the minister to give consideration to a provision in contracts after this date so that subcontractors will be protected against unnecessary losses. When they enter into private contracts they all expect some risk, but they at least know what the risk is and they know there is one way in which they can protect themselves, namely by the provisions of the mechanics' liens acts in the several provinces.

speechtext: the second reading of Bill No. 340, respecting Canadian Nurses' Association.

subtopic: CANADIAN NURSES' ASSOCIATION
speechtext: May we have an explanation?

subtopic: CANADIAN NURSES' ASSOCIATION
speechtext:
In sponsoring this amendment to the Canadian Nurses' Association Act, which was passed by this house in 1947, I should like to say first that the objects of the association as set forth in the act are:
(a)	to dignify the profession of nursing by maintaining and improving the ethical and professional standards of nursing education and service;
(b)	to encourage its members to participate in affairs promoting the public welfare;
(c)	to promote the best interests of the nurses of Canada and to maintain national unity among them;
(d)	to encourage an attitude of mutual understanding with the nurses of other countries; and
(e)	such other lawful acts and things as are incidental or conducive to the attainment of the above objects.
The purpose of the amendment is to include the association of registered nurses of Newfoundland in the Canadian Nurses' Association. There is no change in the act at all except in section 6, which reads:
The following associations or their respective successors and assigns shall be association members;
Then follows a list of the different provincial nursing associations throughout Canada. As I say, the main object of the amendment is to incorporate the association of registered nurses of Newfoundland into the Canadian Nurses' Association, and to do that it is necessary to amend section 6 of the act to include that provincial association.
There is another small change in connection with the association of nurses of Prince Edward Island, whose name has recently been changed from the registered nurses' association of Prince Edward Island. Also the association wishes that the provincial associations which make up the Canadian Nurses' Association be in alphabetical order. That is the only change.
I think the bill is non-controversial. I am sure the house does not want me to make a speech on the work of the Canadian Nurses' Association in alleviating suffering and so on. It is a pleasure for me to sponsor this bill, because it is one more evidence of the desirability of the association in Newfoundland being affiliated with the Canadian Nurses' Association and thereby, perhaps in a small

Private Bills
way, giving evidence of a continuation of the cementing of union which took place in 1949.
I have nothing further to say on the matter. I have endeavoured to explain the purpose of the bill, and I leave it to the sympathetic consideration of the house.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and referred to the standing committee on miscellaneous private bills.

The house resumed, from Tuesday, March 9, consideration of the motion of Mr. Hunter for the second reading of Bill No. 325, to authorize Niagara Gas Transmission Limited to construct, own and operate an extraprovincial pipe line.

Mr. Speaker, when this bill was last before the house I was making a few observations and pointing out that it was hard for me to understand the unplanned manner in which franchises in connection with the transmission of natural gas were being handled by the government. The bill now before the house would grant permission to pipe natural gas from the Niagara peninsula to Toronto, and in my judgment it would be detrimental

to the best interests of the all-Canadian pipe line for which a franchise has already been granted.
There are main lines already in the embryo stage, and if they are to justify their existence they will have to have markets for the gas to be transmitted. In my opinion the branch line covered by this bill to pipe gas into Toronto will interfere with the function of the main line. In view of the development that has taken place, I look upon a bill such as this as merely a method of blackmail. If this franchise is granted it will place the people who hold it in the position where they can sell stock and then offer to sell out. I cannot see the justification for this bill in view of the fact that a franchise has already been granted for the construction of a main line which will need the market in Toronto if it is going to be a paying proposition and not be a development which will have to be heavily subsidized by the Canadian people.
My main objection to the whole development in the use of natural gas is that it is an advance in the use of fuel which should have been more carefully planned. It is all right to get up in the house, as some hon. members do, and say that you cannot stop progress, that with this technological advance other fuels are going to fall by the wayside. That statement is most unrealistic when you consider that there are sections of this country which are going to be hurt by the development of natural gas.
I pointed that out when the proposal was made to pipe Alberta gas to the cities of Montreal and Quebec. I asked the committee which was considering the bill and the witnesses who were appearing at that time if any survey had been made east of Montreal into the repercussions from the use of natural gas in that area. I was told that no survey had been made. I asked the committee and the witnesses if they were aware of the fact that at least two of the provinces east of Montreal depended to a large extent upon the coal industry, one almost completely.
I do not consider that a national project is in the best interests of this country if certain sections are going to be injured or thrown into complete economic chaos without consideration being given as to what compensations are going to be made in that area for the acceptance of what is loosely termed a technological advance.
What about the rest of the country?

The rest of the country is being taken care of-that is what I am objecting to-without any consideration being given to

the parts of the country that will be affected.
I am sure if my hon. friend who has just interjected was living in a part of the country where he had investments in property, in schools, in homes and industry, he would be the first to get up and protest against a development which would wipe out his investments.

I have the utmost
sympathy.

I am sure he is capitalist enough to take that attitude, that he is Conservative enough not to consider the rest of the country if it affected his own individual interests. I would remind the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) who is piloting this bill through the house-

I would like to remind hon. members that while we are considering the bill, over in the Copeland building in this city the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Prudham) is meeting with representatives of the mine workers' union from Nova Scotia and the coal operators from Nova Scotia, in addition to representatives of the provincial government. They are discussing the future of the coal industry in the maritime provinces, because they realize that within a few years the Quebec and Montreal areas will be served with natural gas. That will mean displacing the only economic market for maritime coal in existence at the present time. It also means the wiping out of not only the Dosco shareholders' investment in the coal industry but also of the economies of the communities which are based on coal, and to a large extent disrupting the economic future of these provinces. I would also like to remind hon. members that Nova Scotia is the province which brought the rest of Canada into confederation, and it should be shown more consideration than it has received up to the present time.
Was it not Prince Edward Island?
They held a meeting on Prince Edward Island, but the leadership came from Nova Scotia.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Prince Edward Island was only the cradle.

I cannot see how this kind of development can be termed technological advance. I would ask the members of the
12. 1954	2949
Niagara Gas Transmission Limited committee, when this bill comes before them, to give very careful consideration not only to the benefits which certain sections of Ontario and Quebec may enjoy through the provision of cheaper fuel, but also the hazards which are inherent in that development. I would remind hon. members who represent Montreal and Quebec that the provision of a 3,000-mile pipe line for the supply of natural gas will also mean adapting all your heating equipment to that type of fuel. That alone presents many hazards. Any number of difficulties might arise; the development of available supplies is merely guesswork at the present time, and no one can estimate how long these supplies will last. No one can say immediately with any degree of accuracy that we have sufficient fuel to supply all of Canada and parts of the United States adjacent to Alberta. That angle has to be taken into consideration.
I would also ask the committee to consider the statement made by the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys as reported in a recent issue of an Ottawa newspaper. In that statement he warned those interested in the future supply of fuel not to be in too great a rush to close down the coal industry of Canada. He pointed out, and rightly so, that if you close down mines in which the people of Canada have a huge investment it will be impossible to open them up again very quickly. My experience has been that if you close a mine for six months, then it is almost impossible to open it again.
The minister also pointed out, quite rightly, that we are living in a disturbed and uncertain world. No one can predict how long we will continue to live in peace and security, and in that uncertain future anything might happen. The minister also pointed out that in the event of this country or this continent facing a war, coal would be needed almost as badly as it was needed during the last war, when the government had people running around this country digging gopher holes in order to obtain the necessary fuel to keep the war effort going.
The minister in that statement took a thoroughly realistic position on this subject. For the information of those hon. members who may be on the committee which will consider this bill, I would point out that the whole development of natural gas, oil, coal and hydroelectricity should in the past have been welded into one national fuel policy administered by a board capable of analysing the subject and determining which fuels are most economical. That has been done to a limited extent, although haphazardly, and I would like to point out to members of that

Niagara Gas Transmission Limited committee, if they do not already know, that after pondering that question for some years some of us in this house believe that is the only policy which can cope with the situation. There is already an interdepartmental committee composed of experts on fuel considering this entire question of a national policy, so we should not be in too much of a hurry in passing bills of this kind.
We have a national pipe-line act already in existence under which the government has certain obligations, and it is my belief that any more bills of this nature would be unrealistic until such time as that committee has had an opportunity of examining the whole question and advising the government as to what is required.
Another matter which should be given consideration in relation to this fuel question is the development of atomic energy. The rush to spend millions of dollars and uproot communities in the fuel field is rather shortsighted, particularly when one considers what is going on in Britain. They are at present using pilot plants in certain industries to obtain the necessary data as to how well particular types of fuel operate under given conditions. Submarines have been powered with certain types of fuel. In fact one was launched quite recently.
What would that do to the maritimes?
I am coming to that.

speechtext: Order.

1 do not like to interrupt the hon. member's speech or prevent him developing the broader aspects of his argument, but we are talking on the general subject of pipe lines, and I suggest that he is going rather far afield when he starts discussing atomic energy and matters of that nature. I would ask, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member confine himself a little more closely to the bill.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the hon. member's point, and I am quite willing to co-operate with him. What is wrong with our whole approach to this problem is that in the past, rather than considering the picture as a whole, we have considered the interests of a few people who wished to promote a pipe line. I am sure the average citizen in Ontario did not ask for this pipe line. It took a few promoters to start the ball rolling.
I do not believe you can discuss the development of natural gas, oil, or hydroelectricity without considering the entire fuel picture, and I suggest that we should be a little bit cautious in this regard because it appears to me that the time is not far distant 

when the money we are now spending on fuel may prove to have been wasted, and that it would have been better used in a government-sponsored atomic energy project.
My hon. friend asked what it would do to the maritimes. That is exactly the point I was leading up to in this whole discussion. The one place in Canada where a test should be made with atomic energy is in the maritimes, where there is a shortage of power and where, because of that shortage, it is difficult to establish subsidiary industry. The government is now making an examination of the possibilities of thermal power. That is a long-term process. I think, however, that the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys and others in the cabinet should now consider the possibility of establishing a pilot plant based on some industry in the maritimes in order to determine the possibilities for atomic energy in that field, as is being done in the United States and in Britain.
Mr. Speaker, I merely wanted to say this. My main plea is that when this committee meet to study the terms of this bill, they should look at it in its relationship to the national pipe line that we have already decided upon. Is this duplication? Is it stock promotion? Is it an attempt to grab a field which is lucrative and which might be sold to the main line when it comes through? Do not forget that a government interdepartmental committee today is studying the whole question of fuel with the end in view of a national fuel policy.
Let us not do anything in a hurry. Let us at least wait until some pronouncement is made by that committee as to the economic possibilities of fuels in all fields across this country. I am sorry if I wandered a little bit off the path, but in order to discuss the matter properly I think it was necessary to put the whole thing in its proper perspective.

Mr. Speaker, I just want to say a word or two on this bill. It seems to me that it raises several important points. First of all, the onus is on the sponsors of this bill to show clearly-much more clearly than they have yet shown-that if they are successful, this project will not prejudice the national pipe line which is already under way. I did not read this bill as carefully as I might have, but I have not understood it yet. I personally have no objection at all to the general proposition behind this bill, provided it can be clearly shown that it is not going to prejudice the national pipe line on which we are all depending so much.
There is one point I should like to make. We in British Columbia are hoping for a pipe line of our own before too long. It

just might happen that unless favourable consideration is given to this particular bill our friends in the United States would not be so disposed to give favourable consideration to the application which we shall soon make to have gas piped down to Vancouver and then on into the state of Washington. We cannot have a practical proposition in British Columbia unless we also have that state of Washington market.
There are one or two remarks I should like to make with regard to the statement of the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis). I do not believe we can consider pipe lines in Canada intelligently unless right from the beginning we face the fact that they will have a most vital effect on the future of the coal industry of this country. I think it is impossible to discuss this or any other pipe-line bill without admitting that fact right from the very beginning. I believe the welfare of the coal industry in Canada is of vital concern not only to the hon. member for Cape Breton South and the people of Nova Scotia but also to us in the west. The hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) is certainly going to be affected by the growth of pipe lines and their competition with the coal mines in his riding. My hon. friend who sits to my right is also going to be affected with regard to the coal mines in Fernie.
In this house not so long ago we heard about the way the coal industry is now coming back and facing up to the competition it has been getting from the dieselized railways. It seems to me that it would surely be in the national interest if everybody in Canada began seriously to consider just how coal can hold its own in competition with the new fuels such as natural gas and oil.
I for one do not agree with the hon. member for Cape Breton South on this one particular point only. I believe it is absolutely in the interests of Canada to bring the coal industry back and keep it back. But surely there is a responsibility upon the coal interests themselves. The natural gas interests are coming here, but they are not asking the government to do everything. Surely the coal interests themselves could begin to set their own house in order. Surely the coal interests of Canada, perhaps assisted by the national research council, the dominion fuel board or something like that, could undertake the development of such things as the gas turbine. I should like to see the coal industry and/or the national fuel board or the national research council take into consideration such things as central
12, 1954
Niagara Gas Transmission Limited heating plants for whole municipalities. There is a successful one-and it has been operating for many years-in Lockport, New York. From my friends in Winnipeg I know they have one that I believe is partially successful. As far as I could find out, the chief kick is that it is turned off too soon in the spring, and then the people who are dependent upon it have no heat.
It seems to me that if we had intelligent research into how to bring back coal on a large-scale basis, perhaps coal could hold its own in competition with these new fuels. Why do we use these new fuels like oil and natural gas? Certainly it is not entirely because the new fuels are cheaper than coal, because in a good many cases oil and natural gas are much more expensive than coal. In my own home in Vancouver I burn artificial gas and have done so for 12 years. It is much more expensive than coal or sawdust would be, but of course we bum it because of the extra convenience.
My point is that you cannot separate such things as an application for a particular pipe line for Ontario from the pipe-line picture in Canada as a whole; and in my opinion you cannot separate the pipe-line picture in Canada as a whole from the whole question of fuel and coal.
My hon. friend from Cape Breton South is 100 per cent right on that matter. It is in the interests of the whole economy that we should keep the coal industry healthy and vital; but I think the main onus is on the coal industry itself. It is facing modern competition in a modern age, and it must get busy and fight for its own interests. It must not, for instance, wait for the railways to be dieselized and then, ten years later, begin to come back with things like the gas turbine. If the coal industry would get on its toes like these oil and natural gas boys, perhaps the coal industry would not have so much to fear.

The Social Credit members of this parliament, Mr. Speaker, have followed very closely the statements which have been made with respect to this bill concerning the Niagara Gas Transmission Company. Reference has been made also to the desirability of the Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited project. We do not think it is necessary for us to be long-winded in making our position clear. We were pleased to hear the views expressed by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), as well as those of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew). They

Niagara Gas Transmission Limited stated that the building of this line would have a tremendous and positive economic impact on Canadian life.
We believe it is relevant to this debate to restate that the Social Credit government of Alberta, acting as guardians of the people's resources, has consistently stated their willingness to share their great gift, this natural gas, with the other parts of Canada provided the present and future requirements of the people of Alberta be fully protected at all times, both in the economic and supply sense. When an amount of gas has been established over and above the requirements of the province, then and only then would the Social Credit government approve the export of gas if it was evident that this would be in the best interests of the people of Alberta and the people of Canada.
We have been very consistent in our gas and oil policies. We advanced them many years ago, long before the other political parties realized their value and it became expedient for them to also adopt those policies. As a matter of fact we were constantly abused and criticized by the remnants of the old parties operating in Alberta for the stand we took. I should like to remind this house that in the last provincial election the entire Liberal attack was based on opposition to the export of surplus gas. I believe we should have no more of this political nonsense as to the fatherhood of a sensible oil and gas policy. The truth of the matter is that it was originated by the Social Credit government of Alberta, certainly not by those who now appear so eager to be given credit.
On page 2725 of Hansard for March 5, 1954, the Acting Prime Minister stated that if parliament passed this private bill the government would cease to have jurisdiction over the situation. In view of this fact, and since it is important not to interfere with the proposed pipe line from Alberta, the building of which depends upon its economic feasibility both from the standpoint of the consumer and the producer in the west, I feel it would be a wise and profitable move for the federal authorities to secure the views of the Alberta government on this matter, as well as those of the principals of Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited.
The sponsors of this bill have signified their willingness to switch to natural gas from Alberta when it becomes available. If that is so, then I think more than just a verbal assurance is required. This is a matter which deals with the national interests of the people of Canada, and I believe we should take every precaution to see that nothing is done in this parliament or by any pressure

groups which would jeopardize the building of what is presently considered most desirable, namely the trans-Canada pipe line.

This is the sixth year, Mr. Speaker, in which the members of this house have listened to a pipe-line debate. As I sat here during this debate it seemed to me there was something missing. Of course that "something" is my old and distinguished friend George A. Cruickshank, the former member for Fraser Valley.
He talked himself out, too.

He, more than anyone else, made the pipe-line debate a popular thing. I think they drew larger crowds than any other debates, except the budget debate. In addition, right from the start he had the vision of what could be done for this nation by an all-Canadian pipe line. He had the courage to fight for that project, even against the members of his own party, showing the same courage which he showed to such a wonderful degree in the 29th battalion with which he served during the first world war.
With regard to the question of who is to have credit for the all-Canadian gas policy, I was somewhat surprised to hear the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) stake out a claim to that distinction when he spoke on March 9.
A lot of people are trying to get on the bandwagon.

His remarks will be found on page 2817 of Hansard for that date. I am not anxious to start a political fight, and I merely bring this up by way of setting the record straight. The right hon. minister said this:
In the first place, a private member's bill should be considered apart from politics. If it were not I would be tempted to congratulate the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) for having adopted Liberal policies with reference to oil and gas pipe lines.
Well, of all the nerve; I think that takes the medal.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I am worried
about that.

So am I. Under this plan
Alberta gas is to be piped through Saskatchewan and Manitoba to Ontario and Quebec, with great benefit not only to the western provinces but also to all parts of Ontario and to the Montreal area of Quebec, as well as possibly the Quebec city area.
As the minister said the other day, this development will mean the expenditure in Canada of up to a billion dollars, and of course it cannot help bringing work for many thousands of our people. In central Canada the Alberta gas will partially replace United States coal. I suggest to the house that one of the weakest spots in the Canadian economy down through the years has been the fact that the heavily populated provinces of Ontario and Quebec have been largely dependent upon United States coal. I believe this bringing of Canadian natural gas into
12.	1954
Niagara Gas Transmission Limited Ontario and Quebec will strengthen the nation as no other development in recent years has done.
But as the minister pointed out, and as is generally agreed by all members, the Toronto market for natural gas is essential to this development. If that market is taken by United States gas, other than for a year or two, I suggest such action may be fatal to the whole plan for an all-Canadian gas line policy. Hence the great importance of this bill, because it is this Niagara Gas Transmission Limited which is proposing to bring United States gas into the Toronto market.
I realize, of course, that Niagara Gas Transmission Limited is only a subsidiary of Consumers' Gas Company of Toronto, and of Tennessee Gas Transmission Company of the United States. The plan of this company will mean that United States gas will reach the Toronto market. In my view, at the same time there would be some benefit to an all-Canadian line, because such action would help to build up in the Toronto area a market for natural gas from the west. But as the minister has intimated, the house must try to prevent any action which will kill the trans-Canada plan.
I do not agree with him when he suggests that the responsibility rests entirely with the house. I believe there is a far heavier responsibility on the government because, after all, the government is in a position to make absolutely certain that nothing will be done by Niagara Gas Transmission Limited which will interfere with the all-Canadian plan. And, as in respect of other measures, the government cannot escape final responsibility.
It is worth while to take a look at the plan of Consumers' Gas Company of Toronto, as it is set out at page 2720 of Hansard by the hon. member for Parkdale, who is sponsoring the bill. He has stated that Consumers' Gas made contracts with suppliers of gas in the United States, and in addition made a contract with Tennessee Gas Transmission Company for the piping of that gas to the middle of the Niagara river. The hon. member will correct me if I am wrong in any of these statements. Apparently the contract is for a 20-year period, not just a year or two.
After obtaining that contract Consumers' Gas or Niagara Gas Transmission Limited, I am not sure which, went to the federal power commission of the United States and obtained permission for the export from that country of a certain quantity of natural gas on a 20-year basis. Again this was not on the basis of only a year or two. I believe this permission was obtained at prices set by the

Niagara Gas Transmission Limited federal power commission, prices which were higher than those in the adjacent area of New York state.
Not "set"; approved.

All right; "approved". And now I believe there is an application before the federal power commission in the United States for an increase in that price. My information is that no decision has yet been reached.
The permission is for the Toronto area only. In other words it does not extend to Hamilton, Niagara Falls or St. Catharines; only the Toronto area. That is the only area, of course, in which Consumers' Gas has a franchise. And we must remember that any order made by the federal power commission is subject to further order, depending always upon demands in the United States. Down through the years their decisions have been to this effect, that where anyone residing in the United States can prove a need for gas being exported, such person shall have the right to obtain that gas, and in those circumstances exports to Canada can be cut down accordingly. I believe this has happened in respect of exports to western Ontario. In that area Canadians had the experience of having their gas supply reduced by order of the federal power commission, because some people in the United States were able to prove they needed extra gas.
Apparently, after obtaining this approval from the federal power commission, and because of the insistence that the plan of Consumers' Gas must fit into the all-Canadian plan, Consumers' Gas made a subsequent contract with the Tennessee company. This was referred to by the hon. member for Parkdale when he said, as reported at page 2720 of Hansard:
However, a contract has now been made between Tennessee Gas Transmission Company and Consumers' Gas Company of Toronto whereby over the period of the twenty-year contract between Consumers' Gas and the United States suppliers, Tennessee Gas Transmission Company will purchase all or any of this gas at any time. This latter contract was made so that if-
And I draw attention to that word "if"
-Canadian natural gas is brought to Toronto the Consumers' Gas Company can-
And I draw attention to the word "can", and suggest it can be fairly interpreted as meaning "can, if they wish"-
-purchase Canadian gas and dispose of the United States gas for which they have contracted, without any loss to Consumers' Gas.
On the next page the hon. member says:
-if and when Canadian natural gas becomes available-

So there is nothing binding upon Consumers' Gas or Niagara Gas Transmission Limited to take Alberta gas.
There will be.

That may be, but there is not at the present time. The result is that if this bill is passed, Consumers' Gas or Niagara Gas Transmission Limited can probably block an all-Canadian route. They have already tried to do that. I think the minister knows that last year Consumers' Gas published a number of advertisements about natural gas, some of which I have here from which I propose to quote. From the first I read this paragraph:
The only logical and economical source of natural gas for Toronto is the United States. What always has been true of coal is also true of gas.
Then from another:
It is the opinion of this company and of outside experts that the attempt to bring Alberta natural gas to Toronto is at present uneconomic and therefore not in the public interest.
And another:
Tentative suggestions about natural gas from elsewhere, in the opinion of the company and of outside experts, are for such a high price that the gas could not be sold in sufficient quantity to justify the cost of the pipe line.
There is another which is quite touching, in that they base their argument on their desire to help British Columbia and Alberta. It says:
To help Alberta
Plan of Consumers' Gas to bring natural gas from the United States will help, not hurt Alberta's problem in selling its surplus natural gas and in developing it oil resources.
Careful and expert study indicates that Ontario cannot get Alberta natural gas at prices likely to promote large sale. At the same time if import of Texas gas is prevented by government, it is highly probable that U.S. authorities would be disinclined to permit Alberta gas to enter the northwestern states, the most populous market nearest to Alberta.
All authorities agree that the Vancouver market is not large enough to support a trans-mountain pipe line. So a decree preventing Consumers' Gas from getting United States gas can result in Vancouver not having any natural gas.
That was a pretty far-fetched argument but it does show the attitude of this company just a few months ago. However, on December 4, we had a statement by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and I am reading from the Ottawa Journal, in which he had this to say:
Mr. Howe said the government was undertaking to bring the two western pipe-line companies together to put through the one 30-inch trans-Canada main to central Canada.
By the way, the Minister of Trade and Commerce has been successful in bringing

about a shotgun marriage between Trans-Canada Pipe Lines and Western Pipe Lines. The dispatch goes on:
"The all-Canada line is going to be built, let's have everybody understand that", said Mr. Howe.
And further:
"If Consumer's gas can fit into the Canadian picture all right; if not, then no good", said Mr. Howe.
I find that a similar statement was made by the minister, as reported in the Vancouver Province, on January 5 of this year. The report says:
On the controversial subject of whether Consumers' Gas Company Toronto should be allowed to bring in United States gas before completion of the cross-Canada pipe line, Mr. Howe said the government still holds the view that Consumers' would have to fit into the over-all Canadian plans.
Mr. Howe said the Consumers' import plan has not been ruled out, but he expressed doubt about two points concerning the Toronto company's plans.
These are two points which should be kept in mind by hon. members:
1.	He did not think it could bring gas into Canada more economically than western Canadian gas.
2.	He was not sure of the economics of using the proposed Consumers' line to send Canadian gas southward once the cross-Canada line was built.
In any event, as a result of that stand taken by the minister Consumers' Gas Company now say they will take Alberta gas when it comes east, and will reverse the flow through their pipe lines to the United States.

I do not think that at any time Consumers' Gas said they would reverse the flow of gas through their pipe lines to the United States. They simply said they would change from importing United States gas and take the Canadian gas.

Yes; perhaps I did not put it as clearly as I should have. They say now that they will take Alberta gas. They want the United States gas for the first year or two; then when the Canadian gas comes through they will take it, and their pipe line can be used to pipe the Canadian gas down into the United States.
When the minister spoke in the house on this bill he made it very clear that he was unable to give a guarantee that that result would be brought about. For example, at page 2725 of Hansard he said:
However, this is a private member's bill asking for the incorporation of a company to build a pipe line.
Incidentally, I point out to the minister that they are not asking for incorporation. The company has already been incorporated under the Ontario company law. I continue:
No import permit is required to do so and if parliament passes this bill the government as such
Niagara Gas Transmission Limited would have no control over the situation. It is true that the bill must go to the board of transport commissioners, which, as hon. members know, is a judicial board. I sincerely hope the board of transport commissioners will be seized with the long-range problem of bringing gas to Ontario and Quebec and will measure the effect of the application made under this bill with regard to the over-all results.
I would emphasize, however, that once this bill is passed the machinery operates as set out in the Pipe Lines Act, and no further federal government authority of any kind is required. If the board of transport commissioners should decide that no regard should be paid to the situation brought about by plans to bring gas from western Canada, the government would be powerless to intervene.
He said the same thing when he spoke on March 9, at page 2817 of Hansard, in opening his speech that evening:
Mr. Speaker, before I adjourned the debate when this measure was last before the house I pointed out that the government is unable to give the guarantee sought by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) that the interests of Trans-Canada Pipe Lines will be protected. I pointed out that this measure is a private member's bill. The bill will be examined in the appropriate committee. It will then be returned here for third reading, and after the bill becomes law, all the decisions having to do with the project covered by this bill as well as the project covered by the Trans-Canada Pipe Lines bill will be in the hands of the board of transport commissioners, whose decision will be final.
Then he suggested, as reported at page 2818 of Hansard, that as a remedy there should be what he called a "coming into force" clause which, if I understood him correctly, meant that this private act should not come into force until an agreement between Consumers' Gas and Niagara Gas Transmission Limited, or both, and Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited had been duly executed and deposited with and approved by the board of transport commissioners. Obviously the minister was, and I presume still is. uncertain about the effectiveness of that proposal. I think the objective he had was to see that the trans-Canada line was not interfered with, but he is not yet sure of the best method of realizing that intention. He said:
That is only my suggestion; there may be others.
I propose to make one or two suggestions as to what could be done to bring about the result which is desired by the minister and myself, and I think by nearly everyone in this house.

360. Departmental administration, $821,732.

I should like to make some comments on this item. During the years I have been in this house I have found the public works estimates to be somewhat unique. The predecessor of the present minister, of whom we were all very fond, seemed a creature so far remote from bricks, mortar and such things that one really felt the public works estimates were more in the realm of poetry and romance. So this afternoon when the minister told us he had nothing to say I began to fear that we were again going to be in that delightful world where we were treated with the greatest courtesy but where we found at the end that we had got very little information. I have never quite understood how the minister was able to carry us along so gently and deposit us at the end of the course not much wiser than we were before.
Certain tributes have been paid to the new minister today which interested me a good deal. I would not say for a moment that they were not fully justified, but I think we must be careful that we do not allow the new minister to deal with us in the same way as his predecessor. We have had the minister pictured to us this afternoon in baseball terms as being a man who catches everything, and then there was also a suggestion about delivery. I noticed that while the hon. member for Fort William paid a high tribute to the minister, which I am quite sure was genuine and might have been taken to be disinterested, he did murmur something about a breakwater and other more mundane things which I think he hoped the minister would also be interested in.
There was one thing the hon. member for Fort William said which interested me a good deal. He spoke about the great advantage of not having too much weight, and I mean physical weight. He seemed to think that was an advantage, and indeed I would like very much to agree with him and hope he is right.
When the minister was speaking to us I was interested in some of the phrases he used, and which I took down carefully. I gather that the department he now heads is being "re-established as the government's agency in the field of public works." The


word "re-established" of course raises certain thoughts in one's mind. One wonders what the Department of Public Works had been doing these last several years, but at any rate it is nice to think it is being re-established. It is also nice to think that the Department of Transport is considering-only "considering"-transferring some of the construction it carries on to public works. At any rate that is a beginning, and one hopes the minister will be able to continue it and that some day the Department of Public Works will really be the agency of the government in the field of public works, which some of us were naive to believe it always should have been.
I want to make one or two general remarks about the estimates, because after all these are part of the total estimates which we have had put before us. It is with regard to those total estimates that I want to make some observations at the outset. I want to point out a fact which everybody knows, that government expenditures have gone up. The only reason for this that I can imagine is that the government really does not believe the people are much worried about expenditures. Indeed, I have heard it put much more strongly than that, that the ordinary taxpayer likes to have lots of money spent and that you do not win elections by economy. Indeed, I heard a man say the other day that no election had even been won by economy or by an argument for economy. I do not like to believe that, but I quote it as the opinion of a man who has had some experience with elections. He expressed that with great vehemence.
Having said that; having said that I think the government must hold that view when it brings us estimates so much larger than they have been except in the realm of defence, I am going to make reference to two or three expressions which I hope represent public opinion more accurately than this attitude which, rightly or wrongly, I have attributed to the government. I have here the Edmonton Journal of February 8, which contains an article entitled "Where's the Economy Axe?" I read briefly from it as follows:
Hopes for any federal tax reduction in the 195455 fiscal year have faded with the publication of the estimates Friday. The government is apparently committed to the highest program of spending in Canada's peacetime history-a total of $4,491,751,000. We are left also with the unpleasant thought that, with supplementary estimates, the eventual total may be much larger, perhaps up to the highest level of the war years.
Then I read further from the same editorial.

May I rise on a point of order and ask you, Mr. Chairman, whether

it is in order to discuss the whole field of the estimates on vote 360, which is the administration vote of the Department of Public Works?
I was a little afraid the minister might raise some question of that kind. However, I submit that this is the first item, on which we always have liberty to range pretty far.
Related to the department.

The departmental expenditures are part of all expenditures, and I submit that in surveying the expenditures of the Department of Public Works we are entitled to survey them against the background of the total expenditures. I quite realize that it would not be proper for me to start going into details of the Department of National Defence in remarks on public works, but I do submit that it is perfectly proper to bring to the attention of the minister, who I am sure would like to keep down his estimates to the lowest point and who needs every assistance to that end, what I intend to say. I feel confident that it is relevant to bring to his attention some remarks which have been made about his estimates along with all other estimates.
As long as it is this department's estimates.

The minister will appreciate that I am putting it in that way; the estimate is included in the total figure, and I am referring to that. I would hope, Mr. Chairman, that you will take another view; otherwise you will miss a good deal of a very interesting speech.

I am sorry, Mr. Chairman. I thought you were conceding the relevancy of what I was doing, but I certainly shall not attempt to disregard your ruling in any way.
You have rather cramped my style, Mr. Chairman, but I shall now come to the questions I wish to ask the minister. I shall attempt to be strictly relevant from now on. The minister told us this afternoon in a very interesting fashion of certain changes in method which had been followed. I am not going to run the risk of incurring your displeasure again, Mr. Chairman, but I would like to put it to the minister in this fashion. As the Acting Prime Minister has said, we are in a rather unusual business situation, and we are not quite certain how things will develop. Some of these newspaper quotations 1 was not allowed to read indicated that they also thought this was the time for economy on the part of the government.
It will be recalled that the Department of Public Works estimates, if my memory serves me right, are up by some $7 million. It will be seen that one of the chief expenses is salaries, which bulk very large in the department's expenditures. The minister has come in as what might be termed the head of a large new business which he has taken over. He finds that his staff is increasing substantially. I want to ask the minister this. What steps has he taken to scrutinize that position? I suggest to him-and I think he will agree betause he, like myself, is a reformed busi-nesman-that in a business, if a general manager comes along with a substantial increase in staff, he will be cross-examined by his directors as to what these are for and as to whether he has done everything possible to keep the number down. I suggest

to the minister that this theoretical general manager I am talking about will have to prepare himself for a strict cross-examination as to why his staff is up in number, as I have already indicated.
I want to ask the minister just what steps he has taken. Has he obtained any outside assistance? Has he had any efficiency experts? Or has he just said to himself, "Oh, this is my first year" we will just let things ride along as they are. Then I will have a look at it and I may be able to satisfy myself as time goes on"? Those are the first questions that came to my mind as I read the estimates. Those are the first things that stuck in my mind for answering.
I say again, do we apply one test in private business and an entirely different test in public business? I repeat that I think any executive head of a corporation-especially if times were not too good-who brought in a substantial increase to his staff would be under the strictest cross-examination. I should like to ask the minister if he would just tell us what steps he took before he presented to us these figures which call for substantial additional salary payments.

Mr. Chairman, I just want to speak for a few minutes in this interesting debate. I might say that I enjoyed listening to the discussion this afternoon, because we all look at public works rather from our own experience within our own ridings. I enjoyed the careful analysis of the Department of Public Works administration given by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra.
I was also interested in the information given to the house by the minister. I think it indicates that we are going to have some improvement in the administration of the Department of Public Works. The minister is a competent engineer, and with his qualifications and experience I think he is well suited to head this department assisted by his deputy, who has had a wide experience in military and civilian life. I join with the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra and other members who have expressed their respect for and appreciation of the qualifications and ability of the minister and deputy minister. I sincerely trust that this combination will cure the administrative constipation from which the department has suffered since about 1945.
I have always had a soft spot in my heart for the Department of Public Works. I have known a good many of the officials in British Columbia over a period of 45 years, and the local officials constantly throughout that period. I want to say this. While the work of the senior officials is what comes to the
Supply-Public Works
attention of the House of Commons and the public in general, it is the good work of the hundreds of minor officials in the constituencies that also enables the department to do the work it has done.
I want to refer to two in my own constituency. The first is the clerk of works since shortly after the first world war, Mr. Douglas Male. He happened to be a comrade of mine in A company of the 54th Kootenay battalion. We were wounded on the same day. A lot of good men were knocked out that day. I want to commend the interest he has taken in his work and the effort he has made to satisfy the requirements of the service and yet be courteous to the people, and to meet a lot of unusual circumstances which arise in a constituency and which I am quite sure many of the senior officials know little about.
The other one is Mr. Lomax, whom the hon. member for Skeena knows quite well. He is one of those highly respected Englishmen who never become well off, and throughout the years has acted as inspector of wharves, buildings and various projects. It is the integrity of people like these which has made it possible for the department to do the good work it has done in Kootenay West. He would not allow a contractor to get away with not putting a lock washer on a wharf, or to miss a spike, to put in some poor lumber, or to fail to drive a pile to its required depth.
To do that sort of thing a man has to have some strength of character. He often runs up against people who think that because they have certain political affiliations, certain things can be skipped or overlooked. But here is a man I have known for many years -he retired just recently-and who served the department and the public very well. I mention this matter because the efficiency of the department is to a great extent based on the loyalty and integrity of the junior officials and employees throughout the constituencies. I wish to pay a tribute to the work of these people, who work without recognition.
I recall two or three occasions, because my ranch was adjacent to certain wharves that were being built, where the department took pity on me and realized that I was in a mighty poverty-stricken condition. As a result on a few occasions I was called upon to relieve the supervising inspector when he had to leave a job because of sickness; and on some occasions I met contractors who thought that political affiliations should influence the depth to which a pile was driven, and things of that sort, or just how

Supply-Public Works work should be done. I want to pay tribute to the district engineers we have had in British Columbia. On all occasions, on which a stand has had to be taken against attempted political influence-and I am not suggesting it was official; there is often some selfish person who thinks he has political influence and who wants something improper done on the strength of his political affiliations-I always found the engineers in British Columbia stood solidly against that sort of thing. I think that is a matter of great credit to them, because it is easy to give in to local pressure and permit a little bit of unfairness and scrimping in order to remain popular with some local people. I mention this question because I have had that experience and I think it should be mentioned to indicate the quality of the department's officials.
I was pleased with what the minister had to say with regard to certain reorganization in the department. I have often suggested- and I am speaking with at least some knowledge of the administration of the department in the constituencies-that the public works department was too centralized in its administration. I think the minister will recall that year after year I have suggested that we should have more regional and district administration for the efficient operation of the department. I have often said that, because of local conditions, the local officials should be allowed more latitude to make decisions and meet local conditions. As I say, I have personal knowledge of this matter. I know of several projects that were unnecessarily delayed because certain decisions had to be referred to Ottawa, to the engineering branch, the architectural branch or the legal branch. I believe there should be a regional or district administration of the department, and that the administration should be more decentralized.
I want to illustrate my contention in this respect, and I shall give three or four instances. I know in the last four or five years of the failure of a contractor who had signed a contract to deliver certain lumber and timbers for the building of a wharf. I am now speaking of the Beaton wharf. The failure of the contractor to deliver the lumber in the quantity the local officials required meant that the matter had to be referred to Ottawa, and a new tender called for the delivery of this lumber. The reason for the failure of the contractor to deliver it was that lumber had gone up $10 per thousand after his tender had been accepted. Here we had the public works crew, the piledrivers and other equipment waiting for weeks and weeks, which meant lost time and extra expense. All this occurred because the district officers did not have the power to act in a situation [Mr. Herridge.l

like that. It meant delay and it meant unnecessary expense in the building of that wharf because the district engineer and his officials were not empowered to meet this unforeseen situation. They should have been empowered to immediately purchase lumber at some other point and carry on with the job, rather than have the piledrivers and a crew of men tied up for several weeks while a decision was awaited from Ottawa.
I recall several occasions when the construction of wharves was delayed for months and months because it was necessary for the administration to call for tenders for float logs under wharves. They are difficult to obtain because they are large diameter cedar logs and scarce. Particularly since the war, the lumber operators have not been particularly keen to tender for these logs. The department seems to try to secure a bid for the total number of float logs for the whole wharf, which is almost impossible. The local officials know the small operators, and if a contract called for 200 logs for a wharf they could get 50 from this man and 50 from that man, provided there was authority within the district office of British Columbia to meet a situation like that. This would overcome the delays that have frequently occurred in the past, and on some occasions would have lessened the cost.
Then there is another thing I want to mention. I understand that the department calls for tenders for the construction of wharves, rip-rap, mattress work and works of that sort. Naturally the lowest tenderer is usually given the contract. It often happens that the local officials know that the lowest tenderer has not the capacity or the financial ability or the experience to properly do the job. I know of one wharf that was built in my riding less than three years ago in which the department ran into that situation. In fact I do not think the situation is cleared up yet.
I know of half a dozen men who have lost anywhere from $300 up to $2,000 through supplying goods to these contractors. I feel that in such cases it might be better to let the tender to someone at a higher figure and make sure the work can be completed satisfactorily. In these cases the advice and knowledge of the district officials should be given some consideration, because sometimes the lowest tender does not always mean the job is completed at the lowest cost.
Before I conclude there is one other matter I should like to mention. On one occasion I had to write to the chief architect about holidays for the janitor of the federal building in the city of Nelson. A comparison arose between the holidays of the janitor in Nelson

those of the janitor of the federal building in Trail. Naturally these people get together and sometimes they think they are not getting identical treatment, from their point of view.
I was amazed that the matter had to be referred to the chief architect in Ottawa. I feel that the chief architect is too valuable a man to be looking after janitors' hours, cleaners' hours, and things of that sort. I presume the situation is going to be corrected. If I correctly understood what the minister said this afternoon, a division of property maintenance is to be established, and I presume that division will be in charge of janitors, cleaners, and details of that sort. I think that is a necessary improvement in administration.
I believe the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra gave certain figures which indicated that only about 55 per cent of the total money voted for public works in British Columbia last year was spent. That is clear evidence that the department's administration has been pretty well bogged down. There is no question about that from the evidence. I know there have been a number of revotes in Kootenay West. In fact for three years there was a revote for a wharf at Waneta, which is only a small dock and quite easy to construct. Then we have had delays with the construction of the proposed federal buildings in Nelson and Trail. I shall have more to say on this question at the proper point; I am not going to be out of order now. I do say it indicates that the administration of the department has been slowing down. I believe that condition is general since the war. I know the department has been under tremendous pressure, and I am not criticizing the officials. I blame it on centralization.
I was glad to read in the Ottawa Citizen of February 6 a statement, apparently by one of the senior officials, that this year the government was going to start all projects provided for in the estimates. When the minister replied to the member for Vancouver-Quadra I believe he said something similar, that only those projects were placed in the estimates that the department felt fairly certain of carrying on with this year. I think that is a sound policy, because otherwise you are just fooling the people by putting through estimates year after year and not proceeding with the work.
In conclusion I do urge consideration of my suggestion which I have mentioned for three or four sessions, that there should be a decentralization of the administration of the Department of Public Works. There should be a greater use of the regional or district offices than there is today, and the local officials should be given the opportunity of
Supply-Public Works
meeting unforeseen circumstances of which many senior officials at Ottawa are unaware. I do hope the minister will give consideration to the suggestions I have made, and before the debate concludes I should like to get the minister's opinion regarding them.

I hope you will not call me
out of order, Mr. Chairman, because I have to lay a basis for some of the remarks I am about to make. I was rather surprised to hear the hon. member for Greenwood refer to the free spending by the government. In my personal experience, so far as the Department of Public Works is concerned, it is like trying to draw their eyeteeth to get anything out of them. I have not seen any evidence of free spending in my riding, and certainly not in my province.
Be that as it may, Mr. Chairman, there are one or two things I should like to draw to the attention of the minister. As you know, four years ago we joined with Canada and certain terms of union were negotiated at that time in good faith on both sides. Some of us feel that it is about time some of these terms were put into effect. Our people are under the impression that the federal government is rather dilatory in carrying out its duties in that regard. Under the terms of union, section 33, paragraph
(d), public harbours, wharves, breakwaters, and aids to navigation came under federal jurisdiction.
Section 36 reads as follows:
Without prejudice to the legislative authority of the parliament of Canada under the British North America Acts, 1867 to 1846, any works, property, or services taken over by Canada pursuant to these terms shall thereupon be subject to the legislative authority of the parliament of Canada.
Then on page 35 of the terms of union, under the heading "public harbours"-I think that is public works-we find the following:
It is the policy of the Canadian government to construct and maintain public wharves where and when such action is considered necessary in the public interest. The construction and maintenance of public wharves throughout Canada is within the jurisdiction of the Canadian government and the responsibility for deciding whether or not a public wharf or a breakwater is necessary in any given locality rests with the federal authorities, who take local requirements into consideration.
The Canadian government will, at the request of the province of Newfoundland, and having regard to the best interests of the province, investigate the desirability of establishing one or more harbours in the province as "national harbours" under the national harbours board.
Mr. Chairman, to date there is no sign of establishing any national harbour in Newfoundland; neither do I know of any survey

Supply-Public Works which has taken place there or that is about to take place in connection with this matter.
In this debate reference has been made to revotes, and I know that revotes have taken place so far as Newfoundland is concerned. The hon. member for Greenwood was concerned about the extra staff required. Well, I can say right here and now that the staff we have in Newfoundland is not sufficient to carry out the work, and I think the minister knows it. I want to bring it to his attention again. I do not want to have revotes come before parliament year after year, with nothing done about it. We need in Newfoundland more public servants, and it is the impression of the people in that province that our public services should be brought up at least to the standard of those in the maritime provinces. That is not in the terms of union, but it was understood when the exchange of conversations took place. We are far from that, very far from it.
A low standard.
A very low standard, too low for us. We want to see it improved.

Who said it was a low
standard?

One of my friends to my left.
We want to see our services improved, and we want to live within the terms of union. We would like to see a greater effort being made to carry out those terms of union. The Minister of Public Works, or whoever might hold that portfolio, has to listen to many complaints. But I think the complaints I am making, or the remarks I have been addressing to the committee, are quite justified in the light of circumstances which have developed within the last four years.
The minister paid us a short visit last fall and received a royal welcome. May I say to him, or to his staff, that he should make an extended visit to Newfoundland this summer so he could study the whole public works situation down there. I think he will find that some of the remarks I make tonight will be substantiated. If he were to come we would feel that we are not being neglected, and that an effort is being made to bring our public works at least up to the standard of those in the maritime provinces. If this happens, then under the terms of union our people will feel that they are getting somewhere at last. We are not ungrateful for what has been done, but we feel more should be done. We feel, too, that we are justified in asking for it, under the terms of union.
I do hope the minister will take these remarks into consideration. They are offered


in good spirit, in the hope that the situation in the city of St. John's and other places, so far as federal government agencies are concerned, will be rectified and that we will get the services we desire and which some of us think we deserve.
