speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext: A bigger city.

However, that does not by any means tell the whole story, because you have to subtract from the amount of the estimates the amount of the revotes, and those have been very considerable. We have heard a good deal about them. So far as Calgary is concerned revotes amounted to $316,500, while for Edmonton they amounted to $2,218,000. If you subtract those figures from the amount of the original estimates you find that for Calgary the amount provided was $383,000 while for Edmonton it was $4,267,000.
Your story.

Somebody says that is just my story. Well, if you don't believe it, all

you have to do is take the book of estimates, which I did this afternoon, and jot down the figures, then add them up.
But that is not the whole story, because the total of $383,000 includes the $150,000 in this year's estimates. None of that has been spent up to this time. Then there is a further $100,000 which appeared just before the election in 1949, but which was dropped immediately afterward. So that the total amount spent in Calgary comes to $133,000. That is the total amount for public buildings in that city in the last nine years. I do not know the total amount spent in Edmonton, but from the fact that these sums were being revoted, showing that work was being done, I would judge that most of the amount voted for Edmonton has been actually spent.
These two cities are comparable in size, Edmonton having about 40,000 more population than Calgary. On the other hand Calgary pays considerably more in taxes than Edmonton, and its bank clearances are much higher. In other words a great deal more business is done in Calgary, and probably for that reason there is more need for government offices, particularly income tax offices and the like, which we would be very pleased to get rid of.
Nevertheless, as I have pointed out $133,000 is all that has been spent on public buildings in Calgary in the last nine years, while during the same period of time about $4 million was spent in Edmonton. This, of course, is subject to whatever deductions there may be for some of the items which were not spent. It is clear, however, that no comparison can be made between the amounts spent in these two cities.
Like the hon. member for Red Deer, I have been loath to think that the political complexion of any constituency would cause any difference in the amount of public building that might be carried on. However, the figures I have just placed before the committee indicate that there is something very smelly behind some woodshed, so far as federal buildings in Alberta are concerned. There has not been a fair distribution. The suspicions that I, in company with other people in Calgary, have had in connection with the erection of public buildings, and the possibility of political influence, were not at all allayed by the fact that the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys came down to Calgary before the election and intimated to the people of that city that it would be very much in their own interests to elect Liberal members from Calgary, if they expected to get in on the pork barrel.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, on a question of privilege, I at no time made such a statement in Calgary or anywhere else.
Of course-

-they resulted in two or three editorials being written, as I recall, in both Calgary papers, although one of them is Liberal, upbraiding the minister for trying to bribe the people of Calgary in this manner with their own money. I may say that this statement of the minister in Calgary in regard to this matter probably contributed materially to my returning here at this time.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: Why complain about it, then?
I complain about it because the thing is morally wrong.
Oh, oh.
You would not understand that.

The very mention of
morality causes the Minister of Fisheries to break into loud roars of laughter.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production

His attitude in regard to politics apparently does not take morality into consideration from the word "go". However, a certain number of people in this country both in and out of politics think it is important.
Now, in addition to the fact that this sort of thing is wrong from that point of view, it is also completely unfair. It is unfair as far as the unemployment picture is concerned; it is unfair to the departments of the government which have not adequate or proper space to work in. In 1948 there was an estimate of $100,000 in the public works estimates to make a start on putting up a Department of Veterans Affairs building in Calgary. After the election of 1949, that estimate, having been there for two years, was dropped, or it disappeared, and nothing was ever done about putting up the building. The building has not yet been put up, and the Department of Veterans Affairs offices in Calgary are in three separate buildings. They are scattered about the city, which makes it extremely difficult for them

Supply-Public Works
to carry on business, and extremely awkward for people who have business to do with them, trotting from one building to another to see Department of Veterans Affairs officials. Nothing was done in regard to the matter after that election.
There is another vote of $150,000 which came up last year, and I see there is a revote of $150,000 this year. I am hoping the same thing will not happen to that $150,000 that happened to the $100,000 which was put in before the 1949 election; in other words, that after this year it will not be quietly dropped and we shall hear no more about it.
Until before another election.

Of course the minister is
not responsible for what has gone on over the past nine years, but the government to which he belongs are responsible. They are the people who have been guilty of the discrimination which has taken place out there in regard to the erection of the building; they are the people who are guilty of not putting up this Department of Veterans Affairs building, and as a result inflicting inconvenience on the residents of Calgary and the people of all southern Alberta for many years.
The same thing applies to other government offices. A large number of them in the city of Calgary are scattered about in very inappropriate places, and nothing is ever done about erecting another building. The only building erected there in recent years was between the two elections, and that was a $20,000 weights and measures building, a little bit of a thing. That is all right in its own way, but that is all that has been erected there while those millions were being put into the constituency of the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman permit a question?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext: Can the hon. gentleman tell me where that money has been spent in the city of Edmonton?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: That is what we would like to know.

If the minister does not know where the money has been spent I do not know why he should ask me, because I do not live in Edmonton. All I know is that it was voted and apparently it has been spent there, from what one can make out, on these various projects. One would need to go over the estimates, because there was a revote of a certain proportion of the

original vote in the, next year, which indicated that part of the work was done and a certain amount more was needed to complete it.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext: All we have is a hole for our public building.

Well, then, it is one of the
most expensive holes in history, I would say.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: Next joke, please.
It has had the sum of $4 million poured into it.
They will leave the hole for another election.

They must be trying to dig a hole to sink the city of Edmonton in. In any event, I join with several other hon. members who have spoken in the hope that things will be better in the Department of Public Works from now on. I trust the present minister will go ahead with this particular vote I have mentioned, and also that in deciding where future buildings are to be erected in the province of Alberta he will decide on the basis of the needs of the people there rather than, as apparently has been the case in the past, on the political complexion of the constituencies in the province.

Mr. Chairman, I have three reasons for taking the floor at this time. My first reason is to express on behalf of the people I represent, as well as on my own behalf, our thanks to the minister and his staff for the public works that have been carried out in our province and in my own riding in particular in the past four years.
In this connection I should like to express my own personal appreciation of the sympathetic appreciation and co-operation which I have always received from his officials here in Ottawa, and particularly from his district architect, district engineer and their staffs at St. John's. These people in Newfoundland, as my colleague the hon. member for Trinity-Conception pointed out, are working under very great difficulties, under conditions that do not obtain elsewhere on the mainland, and very often they are working with insufficient staff. I am sure the minister is aware of these difficulties and that everything possible will be done to alleviate them.
My second reason arises out of some remarks made by the hon. member for Van-couver-Quadra earlier this afternoon. My hon. friend drew attention to the small proportion of the vote for Newfoundland that had been spent by the architectural branch, and he suggested that it looked as though some padding had been done in that vote for

electioneering purposes. I can assure my hon. friend that such is not the case. If my hon. friend will look at page 439 of the estimates he will see that out of the 11 items listed under the architect's branch in Newfoundland, seven are revotes. Two of these are in my own riding, and I can assure my hon. friend that one of these revotes is necessary because some unexpected difficulties were encountered in the selection of a suitable site. The other revote was necessary because the plans for the building had not been completed in time to get the work started before winter conditions set in.
We cannot do very much with respect to choosing sites, but the bottleneck with respect to the drawing of plans is the result of the policy of the department of having all those plans drawn here in the head office at Ottawa. This bottleneck could be overcome if the district engineers were permitted to initiate plans and submit them for approval, and then go on and complete them in their own local offices. If this were done I know it would greatly expedite the completion of many of the public works which otherwise have to be carried over. I strongly recommend that for the minister's consideration.
I next would like to draw the attention of the minister to the need for more dredging equipment in Newfoundland. We have only one small dredge which is unsuitable for many of the dredging operations, and which cannot possibly cope with all those for which it is suitable. We really need a second larger and more powerful dredge, as well as some drag-line equipment for small harbours which the dredge cannot enter. I hope the minister will give consideration to these needs as soon as he can find it convenient to do so.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to follow the general argument which was presented this afternoon by my colleague the hon. member for Red Deer, because the particular projects which he brought to the attention of the minister as not being in this year's estimates are located partially in my constituency. We are greatly incensed over the fact that these particular projects were in last year's estimates and now, a year later, have disappeared. The minister gave as a reason for this that he did not feel it was right to place items in the estimates which they were not prepared to proceed with, and then went on to inform us in his amiable way that because they did not appear in the present estimates did not mean that they had been abandoned.
That sounds nice; that sounds lovely, to be told they have not been abandoned, but when they do not appear you can hardly
Supply-Public Works
tell people they have not been abandoned. That phrase can mean anything. We might ask if they are going to be gone ahead with and be told that they have not been abandoned, they may be in there next year or they may be in there five years from now. We are told that they have not been abandoned, and they may be in there 50 years from now or 100 years from now. To be told they have not been abandoned just does not mean anything. What it does mean is that it has been abandoned for this year, and that is what we do not like.
I can understand the desire of the minister to cut out a lot of deadwood from the estimates and not have items there just for the sake of putting them in. However, I would like to ask if there are any projects in the estimates this year which were not approved last year. Are there any public works to be erected in Alberta this year, which are in the estimates this year, which are new items and which were not previously approved? If so, then I think there is something wrong somewhere. I contend that the department is duty-bound to go ahead with projects which this parliament has approved before they enter upon any new projects. If they are going to do that we are just not going to know where we stand at all in respect to these things.
The hon. member for Red Deer pointed out that in last year's estimates there was a group of projects with which the minister was going forward to the extent of acquiring sites if money was available after the other work had been done.
I bring to the minister's attention one particular project in that group, the public building for the town of Claresholm. I met with representatives of the service clubs, the board of trade, the mayor and other responsible citizens, who called me by telephone and asked me to come and look over the situation. They said, "Mr. Hansell, as far as the site is concerned, we have one already". They showed me an admirable site, a corner lot on one of the main streets just a stone's throw from the busiest section of the town. There could not be a better site. They said, "We are prepared to give this to the federal government so they can get started". They offered it to the government, and the last I heard from the minister the papers were being drawn up by the legal branch and the government was taking over the site.
That was real progress, but what is the position now? The position is that the town has handed over a beautiful site to the dominion government, and there is nothing in the estimates to show that they are going

Supply-Public Works forward with the building. They are put back a year, and this government has the property. That is the situation now.
I think the minister should answer that question. While he is thinking about the answer to that I am going to ask him another one. I would like to know if he can give to this house, particularly for the benefit of some of the newer members, particulars of the procedure followed by the government in arriving at projects which they seem to think should have priority. I understand that in the case of public buildings which, generally speaking, involve the housing of post offices, the R.C.M.P. and other governmental agencies, the Post Office Department will submit a number of requests which are then blocked off into groups according to their importance, group A, group B, group C and so on. If that is not right, the minister can tell me.
If there is a priority list of that kind I should like to know if that list remains unchanged or do they say something like this. "Here is one item in group A. We will have to put that back in group B and take something from group C and put it up at the top." Does that ever happen? I cannot see that the situation would change so quickly as to cause that to happen, because these various communities are not changing as rapidly as that.
It seems to me that if there is a priority list, that list should not change very much. It might vary slightly, but not too much. Therefore if there is something in the estimates one year it is reasonable to suppose that if they do not go forward with it that year it will reappear the next year, because it would be that much further on toward the top of the list. I should like the minister to answer those questions for me.
I am not going to say too much about the political significance of these things. I think the government has acted pretty fairly with me and with my constituents except in the case of the group of projects we are now bringing to the minister's attention. They constitute a sore spot. What happened is simply this. They appeared in the estimates, they were approved by parliament, the community said they had a site which they would give to the government. Then there was an election. I am not going to say what happened, but they returned a Social Credit member and the following year the project was missing from the estimates.
That does not look good. We cannot very well go back to our constituents and say, "We hope you get it the year before the next election." That presents a rather embarrassing situation for some of us, and I do not think it can do anyone any good. In addition it is
[Mr. Hansell.l

embarrassing for the government, though I cannot say the government has been unfair as regards my own constituency. Even this year Edmonton received $2 million, which is quite a chunk out of the total of $3,600,000 which goes to Alberta as a whole. The remainder of that money has to be divided up among the other constituencies, and it is obvious my constituency gets a fair share, so I have no complaints to make.
I do not know anything about what the hon. member for Edmonton West did in the last election. I did not follow him around or listen to all he said. I had something else to do. My leader points out that I could not stand it in any case. Nevertheless, in a general election campaign we know something of what is said, because people are going around the different political meetings. I do know for a fact that my opponent said, 'The reason you have not got a public building in this community"-this does not apply to Claresholm but it does apply to two or three other places-"is because you have not been voting Liberal." That was said, but it did not go down with the people. They do not swallow that sort of thing, because it will be noted that I am here and the poor old gentleman who said that lost his deposit. But that sort of thing is pretty low campaigning. I do not believe the minister would agree with that sort of thing, and I would like to think that the Liberal party would not stoop to that low form of campaigning.
I believe the minister should close those mouths tonight and say, "No, sir, we do not agree with that", so that the next time that sort of thing is said we will have the minister's word to the effect that these public works projects are not going to be administered on the basis of whether the government gets support from here, there or somewhere else. If he will make a declaration to that effect it will settle the problem.
Once again I wish to emphasize that I personally have no complaints to make, but I do believe some of these two-by-four politicians going around should raise their sights a little bit and carry on their campaigns not on the basis of pork barrel politics or handouts, but on the basis of great principles. Of course if they have no principles they cannot talk about them, and perhaps that is the reason. Perhaps they do not know of any, but surely we can raise our sights in political campaigns and tell what we stand for and what we propose to do.
I do not wish to say any more, Mr. Chairman, except to ask the minister this question, and I hope we will get a straightforward answer and not the reply that some of these

projects are merely being held over. My question is this. Will he tell us whether there are any new projects which are taking priority over projects which have already been approved by parliament?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Kootenay East.

I wonder if the hon. member for Kootenay East would permit me to answer the specific question asked by the hon. member for Macleod. I can give a specific answer. There are no new projects in the estimates for this year concerning the province of Alberta which have taken priority over projects which were approved in the estimates for last year.
As to the charge, implied or direct, that these projects are determined on the basis of politics, I wonder if the hon. member has, for example, consulted the hon. member for Bow River, or the hon. member for Lethbridge, and asked them if they are in agreement as to whether we have ever determined these projects on the basis of the local candidate's ability to get votes. I believe it will be concluded that we have been fair in our approach to this problem. The hon. member for Red Deer, speaking last night, reminded the house that one of the projects which was dropped was in the constituency of my good friend the hon. member for Athabaska.
As a matter of fact I might tell the committee that my colleague the Minister of Agriculture has just reminded me that one project in his constituency has been dropped.
Is that the post office at Lemberg?

I have forgotten the name. We have been trying to work in conformity with the general policy enunciated. Many hon. members this afternoon and this evening have said that this is a good policy. I believe every hon. member in this house believes it is a good policy, and it will doubtless be regarded as a good policy as long as it does not adversely affect any particular hon. member. But when it does affect a particular hon. member adversely he feels it is not a good policy but rather is based on political partisanship. That is not the way these projects are administered, and all hon. members will realize that once we have an opportunity of dealing with some of these revotes, and actually starting the construction of these buildings and clarifying the estimates, then we can deal with new votes for new projects.
The hon. member for Greenwood spoke about the organization of the department, 83276-188|
Supply-Public Works
and asked what I had done about looking into this situation, and whether I was satisfied with the increase in personnel. He had several other questions relating to administration. I am sure he knows that most of the-increases shown in the estimates were authorized before I came to the Department of Public Works. Indeed, very few have beem authorized since that date. The only substantial recent increases are caused by the transfer of personnel from the Department of Resources and Development in the trans-Canada highway division, and personnel related to some of the other functions which were transferred.
The senior officials of the department and I have been going over various sections of the department very carefully. I have endeavoured to get around the department and speak to all individuals myself. I know the deputy minister has done more than I in that particular field. We recently assembled in Ottawa the chief district personnel of the department-engineers and architects-to discuss with them the whole range of problems with respect to the operation of the department within the scope of their jurisdiction to see how we can make the department more effective, and to what extent we can delegate operations from the headquarters here at Ottawa so as to clear bottlenecks.
As regards the question of whether we have brought in outside management consultants to survey the activities of the department, my answer to that is no. We are endeavouring to get this department into the condition we want it, and that will take us some time. At the moment I have no plans for seeking that sort of outside help.
The hon. member for Kootenay West made his usual good suggestions about decentralization, and I must say I have some of these very points in mind. I believe there should be some decentralization of the operations of the Department of Public Works, and we have already taken some steps in that direction. The hon. member for Burin-Burgeo also dealt with the same point. I thank him for his suggestions. I think that covers the points I have before me at the moment. If there are any others I shall deal with them later.
Before the minister takes his seat, may I ask him to deal with the point raised by the hon. member for Prince Albert? I refer to the Lunam Construction Company matter.

As to the Lunam Construction Company, I may say that we have been engaged in trying to satisfy the claims of the

Supply-Public Works
subcontractors in so far as there is money available for that purpose, and depending upon whether or not they themselves can get together and determine the quantum and validity of their own claims in relation to each other. That is being done at the present moment, and I hope that before too long we will be able to pay to the valid subcontractors the moneys remaining in the hands of the crown for that purpose.

I must apologize to the Chair for my impetuousness, but I wanted to follow my colleague the hon. member for Kootenay West. I wanted to do so, first, because I want to say how highly pleased I am to see him so fit after his serious illness. As he will realize, he is my neighbour. My second reason was that I wished to associate myself with his high praise of the departmental officials and the ministry in general for the efficient manner in which they have handled public works affairs.
There is another matter, however, that I feel is important at this time, having regard to the objections of the other provinces, particularly Alberta, to the absence of large appropriations for their various projects. There is one thing I should like to point out in regard to the matter of unemployment at the present time. It is my opinion-perhaps it is not shared by everyone-that public works at this time in the form of necessary projects would do a great deal to alleviate the bad situation that exists in British Columbia. I have formed the opinion recently that, in relation to all of Canada, the figure in British Columbia in the matter of unemployment is 65 per cent higher than that of the over-all picture.
With that fact in mind, while there is a substantial appropriation for public works in the matter of acquisition and construction of public buildings and so forth, for the trans-Canada highway and other projects, nevertheless I would hope that before the supplementary estimates come down the cabinet would give this matter serious consideration, and that certainly the estimates of the Minister of Public Works would be given careful consideration. I am sure Alberta is not suffering as greatly as is British Columbia in the unemployment situation. Alberta is predominantly a farming and oil province, and there is no recession in that regard.
This afternoon something extremely interesting was raised with regard to the question of whether or not there is favouritism in the matter of public works. I do not think there is, even if the province of Alberta does fall $1 million below British Columbia-I believe the :figure is about $800,000-in this one item that

I am looking at, namely the acquisition and construction of public buildings. In that one item they lack only about $800,000 in order to equal the appropriation for British Columbia. On the other hand the hon. member for Macleod, in an earlier address, pointed out that British Columbia pays to the federal treasury $239 million in round figures, or $45 million more than the total collected from the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta. With that fact in mind it is not a large figure by which we exceed their appropriation.
The hon. member indicated that there was some favouritism, or that he felt there was going to be favouritism, because of the fact that when he went home for the election they were singing some sort of song there. I have not the exact words but I believe they went something like this-
Do you want some music?

-"With Shaw, no public buildings; without Shaw, a federal building". I do not know what the tune was. Perhaps "Home on the Range" would work in nicely. Perhaps it would have had more effect had they been using that tune. On the other hand, I had a highly interesting experience in British Columbia. For some unknown reason my supporters felt that I was not too much needed in my riding, and they sent me into the interior to support a Liberal in another riding. It happened to be a riding held by a member of the C.C.F. party. This, by the way, is in relation to whether or not there is favouritism, or whether the members on either side of the house should feel there is favouritism.
I had made what I thought was a good speech. I do not know whether the audience thought so or not. However, I had given a good account of what the Liberal party had done in the past number of years. I did not say in any way that they had constructed buildings here or there; I gave the over-all picture and did not become parochial in any way. After I sat down one of the gentlemen in the back of the hall stood up and said, "Mr. Chairman, I would like to ask the speaker a question". I said, "Yes?" He said, "The C.C.F. candidate has been going about this riding saying, 'Don't be foolish; don't send a Liberal down there; send one from the opposition'. He had in mind the C.C.F. He said they are the only ones who can really get anything out of the government".
That is the other side of the picture. Whether it is politics or not, certainly I felt that he hit well below the belt. My answer was that that certainly was not so, and that

when a really progressive member of parliament put his case before the government he received the same treatment regardless of whether he belonged to one party or the other. I think it is pretty generally the feeling on the other side of the house that this government is treating all projects with reference to public works, transport or anything else, absolutely on a non-political basis and only on their worth.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext:
Some of the hon. members from Alberta have insinuated that there is not fair treatment in the allocation of public works. The Minister of Public Works has effectively answered that charge. They also made some insinuations. The hon. member for Calgary North and the hon. member for Macleod suggested that during the recent campaign questionable methods were used to get political support.
In that inference I completely agree with the hon. member for Macleod. I would say that there were some extravagant statements made in Peace River by the hon. member who presently represents that constituency. I did not take hearsay for it but procured from the radio station a copy of the script of one of his speeches. I am sorry I do not have it with me tonight, but part of his speech was to this effect. "You do not have to send a Liberal to Ottawa to get public works. Look at your constituency. I got you a new public building. I got you $600,000 for the airport. Look at the two Liberal constituencies, one on either side. They got nothing. If you want public works, send me to Ottawa."
Now, if that is what the hon. member for Macleod means when he says two-by-four politicians go around using questionable means to win political support, I completely agree with him.

After listening to the
interesting remarks just made by the minister I probably will not have very much to say. I should like to express my appreciation of the vote in the estimates which will enable Mackenzie to have our first federal public building in the near future. 1 am sure there are very few members in this house who have not within their constituencies at least one public federal building. My remarks last night might have conveyed the impression that Mackenzie is a God-forsaken part of the world, but it is not. It so happens the constituency is spread over a large area, and about 50,000 people live there. We produce large quantities of grain, timber, minerals and fur.
Mackenzie did have a public building at one time, back in 1874. The first government
Supply-Public Works
buildings in the Northwest Territories were built at Fort Livingstone in my constituency. Then, as now, there were people who were critical of the government's extravagance. "The buildings were erected at a huge cost, but were of flimsy and unsubstantial character, built of lumber and hewn logs." Hon. members might be interested in the huge costs-$5,600. There was to have been a divisional point at Fort Livingstone on the C.P.R. running from Winnipeg to Edmonton over the northern route, which would have been a much better route for the first transcontinental railway, in my opinion.
For some reason or other the Canadian Pacific's plans were changed and the railway went miles to the south, through a much more desolate part of the country. Consequently the government buildings were moved from Fort Livingstone. At that time Mackenzie did boast a public building, but now there is not a single federal public building in the constituency.
I must thank the minister for looking after Kelvington. I hope it was an oversight that resulted in Carrot River, which I understand had been included a year ago, being overlooked this year. I hope that when the supplementary estimates are brought down the minister will take care of that oversight. I might say that I have had several letters from the town clerk, and also I have had some photographs sent along which I shall send to the minister. I would appreciate it if he would keep them until the new public building is erected. Then we shall be able to compare the pictures of the old with the new. I have letters from the secretary of the Carrot River board of trade, and from the minister's colleague, the Postmaster General. The latter wrote me on February 5 as follows:
We have reason to believe that the Department of Public Works may be considering the erection of a public building in which the post office and other government departments would be located.
The present accommodation is not satisfactory, and is being leased by the Department of Public Works only on a monthly basis.
As a result of previous representations and the evident need for improvement, this department is urging the Department of Public Works to provide improved postal accommodation in accordance with our policy for offices in this class.
I might say that Carrot River is the end of steel. If the Minister of Agriculture were here I am sure he would agree with me that it is a very important centre in one of the last frontiers of prairie settlement.
I have been interested to note that there has been a change in government policy since I was here from 1940 to 1949. At that time there were a great many requests from communities for public buildings, and naturally I referred those requests to the proper departments. The replies were that because

Later the policy seemed to be that if the total revenue of the post office was less than $10,000, neither the Post Office Department nor the Department of Public Works would recommend a public building.
This afternoon, while waiting to make these remarks, I have gone through the annual reports of the Minister of Public Works for the years 1951 and 1952. I have noticed that for Yorkton there has been a very large appropriation of $800,000 for an addition to the very fine post office. Centres like Regina and Saskatoon have been getting generous consideration. I think there should be something said for these rural communities that have not any finer type of architecture than the country elevator. I feel that under the new concept of the minister, some of these small communities should have an example of what can be done by a little imagination.
I notice some progress has been made. I was checking over the constituency of Melville, where the minister indicated they are passing up one building. All these places I am about to mention are much smaller than Carrot River. The revenue from the Carrot River post office is $8,508. These places I am going to mention have had public buildings, according to the minister's reports. Lemberg, with a post office revenue of $4,810, has had a new building. Ituna, with a revenue of $5,354, had a new building costing something over $30,000. Fort Qu'Appelle with a revenue of $8,000 had several buildings, the contracts for which were awarded to the Lunam Construction Company. There was a contract for the construction of a public building, $129,000; an Indian hospital for $318,000; a sewage disposal plant for $19,000. Then Balcarres, with a post office revenue of $7,005, apparently had a new building. Lang-enburg, with a revenue of $8,277, had a new public building constructed by the Lunam Construction Company at a cost of $84,000. Saltcoats, with a revenue of $5,676, must have a very modest building because the cost is shown at $75.74.
I would suggest that since the constituency of Melville has been able to get public buildings for centres like Lemberg, Ituna, Fort Qu'Appelle, Balcarres and Langenburg, it is not unreasonable to expect a building in Carrot River. It is not unreasonable to expect that the commitment made a year ago for a new office building should be proceeded with, and that when the supplementary estimates come down before Easter this oversight will have been corrected.


These public buildings serve two purposes. They handle Her Majesty's mail, and they house the representatives of the R.C.M.P. I submit that if Her Majesty should visit the post offices in Mackenzie constituency she would decide that they must have been built in keeping with the times of her great-greatgrandmother, Queen Victoria, because there have not been appropriations that would make it possible for the people in these rural communities to have the public buildings which are taken for granted in the larger cities. I know the Post Office Department has taken the position that the large cities provide the revenue, but in the final analysis the taxpayers of all Canada provide the money for these wonderful public buildings that are being erected in nearly all Canadian cities.
I hope the minister and his staff will give a new look to this department. I want to endorse what has been said by hon. members in all parts of the house, that we have a great deal of confidence in the imagination and the ability of the minister and his staff. And so I hope in the years to come there will be worth-while appropriations for rural constituencies such as Mackenzie where, in the past, we have not been able to get many public buildings.

Mr. Chairman, for the first time since I have the honour of sitting in this house, I have before me the estimates for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1955. When I saw that the Department of Public Works intended to spend $130 million and a few hundred thousand dollars during the coming year, I asked myself for what purpose the government was requesting parliament to vote such a large amount. I came to the conclusion that the government had the duty of providing the Canadian nation with the numerous public services needed to ensure its expansion, development and progress. And secondly-this seems quite important to me- a public works program gives work to those who must provide for a wife and children.
Mr. Chairman, I note with regret that the amount earmarked for public works in Quebec city-I have the honour of representing one of its constituencies-is but $225,000. When I say $225,000 I am being generous because that amount includes $125,000 which is a revote from last year, the money not having been spent.
Mr. Chairman, I wish to draw to the attention of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters) and of the government the fact that the citizens of Quebec city are probably those who are most affected by the unemployment situation now prevailing in Canada.

On November 23 last, I had the honour of making the first speech of my political career in this house. At that time, as will be seen from page 231 of Hansard for that day, I spoke of the working classes I represent in this house. Mr. Chairman, may I quote to the hon. members a few excerpts from that speech which, in my opinion, are quite relevant to the remarks I wish to make tonight. I stated, Mr. Chairman, that:
However honest and generous they may be, our working people must not nevertheless consider themselves as forming an inferior class. It is as honourable as any other class of society. Our workingmen are legitimately proud of what they are. They rely upon their elected representatives to give voice to their legitimate representations.

I thank you for your observations, Mr. Chairman. I want to discuss public works, and in doing so I wish to claim public works for the city of Quebec. I would point out at the same time that I am asking for public works in that city because there is unemployment. In speaking in my mother tongue, Mr. Chairman, I shall do my best to have you understand me by speaking as slowly as possible.

Supply-Public Works In the speech I delivered on November 23 last and to which I again refer, I added:
The workingman, Mr. Speaker, is entitled to the gratitude of the government. To his ability, competence and love of work we owe almost everything that strikes our eye. His rugged hands are evidence and confirmation of the long hours he has toiled in his shop or in the yard, under the burden of his tools. The honest and conscientious worker- and those traits are typical of the worker living in the constituency of Quebec West-is the builder of the nation and it is our duty to recognize that fact.
Mr. Chairman, on the same occasion, and I intend to do it again tonight, I asked the government to undertake in Quebec urgent and necessary public works that were needed and that the government may not disregard any longer today. I ask and I demand as strongly as I can that the St. Charles river be dredged and that the pollution of the Lairet river be eliminated. That is a knotty problem, not for the constituency I represent, but more particularly for the constituency of the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) since these two rivers happen to be in his constituency where, I repeat, they are not only a disgrace for the city of Quebec, the capital of the province of Quebec, but they are also a source of infection for its citizens. I am at a loss to understand why a self-styled Liberal government should not pay more attention to these people. After all they have regularly obtained from them expressions of what I might make so bold as to call blind confidence. If my hon. friends now find themselves sitting on the opposite side of the house, the citizens of Quebec are the ones primarily responsible. Is that the way in which the Liberal government chose to show its gratitude? In that case may I ask them quite simply to stop this joking at the expense of the people of Quebec and to proceed with those works which are needed to cure this unemployment situation.
When the public works estimates are considered, I shall have the opportunity of referring again to the same subject. Tonight I merely wanted to speak on behalf of the province of Quebec and ask what I already asked on November 23 last, when the Right Hon. the Prime Minister was here, that the people of the province of Quebec should get what is needed in that province. This has become a necessity. Both rivers to which I referred a moment ago are a danger to public safety, especially to public health, and I feel that our human resources must be protected if we want Canada to remain great and continue along the path to prosperity.
I read in the newspapers this week a statement which seems to me utterly fanciful; it was reportedly made by the Right Hon. the
